"We must get rid of collusive loan-for-equity-deal assets and negative-asset-value loans as scheduled," the official said. "If we fail to do so, we may face international criticism again and our efforts to restore creditworthiness would be in vain." Loan-for-equity-deals are arrangements in which a company puts up a loan it has received at a bank as collateral when it issues equity. Such deals were collusive because they benefited the companies involved at the banks' expense. Negative-asset-value loans are loans on which banks normally cannot cover their costs through interest income. The efforts by Japanese banks to dispose of problem loans began in the late 1994/95 business year and have continued in the current year to March 31. By the end of the current business year, they are expected to have written off a record total of 6.0 to 6.5 trillion yen ($55.5 to $60.5 billion) of bad loans. response: Japanese workers are facing another year of marginal salary increases as traditional systems of fixed pay rises give way to greater wage flexibility and growing job insecurity. Corporate reforms aimed at reviving the sluggish economy have forced many companies to scrap long-term plans for annual wage increases, which were once a major attraction for workers in Japan. Instead, they are focusing on performance-related pay and short-term incentives to boost efficiency and reduce costs. "The trend towards eliminating fixed-amount annual wage increases is continuing," said Yoshio Hirao, director of the employment policy division at the Ministry of Health and Welfare. "This year, some companies are likely to say they are temporarily suspending the payment of planned annual wage increases." Last year, more than 100 firms temporarily suspended planned wage increases, up from just 10 in 1996, according to the labour ministry. Among them were major firms such as Mitsubishi Electric Corp, NEC Corp and Toyota Motor Corp. This year, more firms are expected to follow suit. A survey by the Nikkei business daily showed that 240 large companies plan to offer only marginal wage increases this year, up from 220 last year. The survey also showed that 130 of those companies have no definite plans to raise annual wages at all. Instead, they plan to focus on performance-related pay and incentives based on improvements in productivity. "Fixed-amount annual wage increases are becoming obsolete," said an official at one large trading firm. "We need to establish a new system of pay that can motivate employees to work hard in the harsh market conditions." Haruo Shimada, an employment analyst at Moody's Investors Service, said that temporary suspension of planned wage increases by some companies this year is inevitable, especially in the finance and real estate industries and among non-manufacturing firms. "But permanent elimination of fixed-amount annual wage increases at those companies is likely to begin next year," he said. Elimination of fixed-amount annual wage increases is particularly dangerous for Japan's big employers, as they already pay their workers higher salaries than their rivals in other countries, analysts say. Last year, average annual wages in Japan's private sector were 23 percent higher than in the United States and 41 percent higher than in Germany, according to the labour ministry. If they want to remain competitive, they must cut the huge wage bill, analysts say. "To maintain their current levels of pay, big Japanese employers must increase productivity by 5 percent each year," said Hiroshi Watanabe, an employment analyst at UBS Securities Ltd. "If they fail to do so, they will be forced to cut jobs." The trend towards elimination of fixed-amount annual wage increases began in the late 1990s, when Japan's major employers were hit by the twin deficits of finance and politics and forced to focus on improving their bottom lines. Last year, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's government unveiled a major reform programme, called "restructuring" or "jigou haikaku" in Japanese, which included plans to scrap employment-for-life and drastically cut the huge social costs, including pensions and medical care, paid to workers. The employment-related reforms are aimed at making Japan's labour markets more flexible so that the nation can effectively cope with the challenges posed by the globalisation of markets. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Editorial/Chris Gallagher Tokyo, 12 October 1997 01:00 GMT Reuters Limited Copyright 1997 Reuters Limited. response: Japanese workers are facing another year of marginal salary increases as traditional systems of fixed pay rises give way to greater wage flexibility and growing job insecurity. Instead of the usual annual increases, companies are expected to focus on performance-related pay and bonuses to keep wages competitive, labour analysts said. "Fixed pay rises are becoming marginal and may even disappear in the long run," said Yoshio Oyama, an analyst at the Moody's Investors Service. "Instead, companies will focus on performance-related pay and bonuses to keep wages competitive." This year, most major companies announced pay rises of less than 10 percent even before the general wage-setting talks between labour and management took place in the spring. The talks, called "shunto" in Japan, involve the country's biggest labour unions and traditionally set pay increases for the year at large companies. Even this year, when the talks were held after a record-long delay due to complex negotiations over reforms at Japan Air Lines and Nippon Steel Corp, the unions managed to secure only marginal pay rises. A Moody's survey found that 78 percent of 120 large companies planned to keep their annual pay-rise budgets unchanged or reduce them in the 1997/98 fiscal year. A credit analyst at Moody's said the trend towards wage flexibility was a positive sign for the companies as it would help them remain competitive in the challenging economic environment. "We welcome the news that some big employers are planning to cut their annual wage-rise budgets," the analyst said. "Such flexibility in wage costs is essential for big employers to stay competitive in the challenging economic environment." The push for wage flexibility comes as Japan faces intensifying competition from cheaper labour markets in Asia and the threat of massive job losses as industries are restructured. Last year, Japan's per capita income fell below that of Switzerland and Belgium for the first time, highlighting the need to boost productivity. The push for wage flexibility also reflects efforts to streamline labour costs in preparation for the expected introduction of a universal health insurance system from April 1997. The system is expected to increase corporate costs by around 1 percent of their annual revenues. However, some labour analysts warned that excessive wage flexibility could lead to a widening income gap between permanent and temporary workers, or between workers at the same company. "Excessive wage flexibility may lead to a sharp income disparity," said Hideaki Shibata, a researcher at the Institute for Labor and Social Security Research. "We must be careful not to widen the income gap between regular and temporary workers, or between workers at the same company." He also urged unions not to give up their efforts to secure reasonable pay rises through collective bargaining. Shibata said unions should focus on securing pay rises for their members, rather than for non-unionised workers, to maintain their existence. However, Rengo Haraundo, president of the Rengo union federation, said unions had no choice but to adapt to the changing environment. "We must adapt to the changing environment, otherwise we will lose our reason for existence," he said. "But this does not mean we will give up our efforts to secure reasonable pay rises through collective bargaining." Haraundo also warned that excessive job-cutting could lead to social unrest. Japan's major trading companies and banks announced huge layoffs last year, and more job-cutting is planned this year. Haraundo said such plans could lead to social unrest if the layoffs were excessive. "If layoffs at major companies are excessive, this could lead to social unrest," he said. "We must carefully watch how these companies treat their workers." #END.

Corporate reformers have long criticised Japan's "lifetime employment" system under which companies promise to employ workers for their whole working lives, even if that means keeping on unproductive staff, in order to avoid the financial and emotional costs of layoffs. But even more critical is the way this system is linked to generous pay rises, or "joretsu" or "fixed-sum" systems, under which workers receive the same amount of extra pay each month from October to March the following year, regardless of their actual productivity. The reforms were aimed at making Japan's labour market more flexible and efficient, especially as the country faces intense competition in markets liberalised under the U.S.-led Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) free trade pact. "We want to keep the motivation among our employees to increase their productivity until the end of the current business year," Ikuka said. Instead of the usual annual increase in base pay, many firms are offering "performance-related" pay rises, or are holding off any decision until the end of the business year in March. "The trend towards eliminating fixed annual pay increases has not stopped but is getting more pronounced," said Chiyoko Ejima, an employment analyst at Nomura Research Institute. "Companies want to keep their options open until the end of the current business year, which is unusual even for the unstable labour market here," she added. Traditional Japanese firms have long offered annual pay increases, known as "juro-shu", which are decided before the start of the fiscal year on April 1. These pay rises are based on an employee's rank or length of service and are intended to keep workers contented and motivated. But with intensified competition from low-cost rivals in Asia, particularly in labour-intensive industries, some Japanese firms are trying to make their wage structures more flexible. Last year, more than 70 percent of firms surveyed by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) offered no juro-shu at all. Instead, they decided on pay rises based on each employee's performance during the year. This year, the proportion of firms without juro-shu is expected to rise further. Among the 1,000 firms which the MHLW asked about their pay-raising plans for this year and last, 80 percent said they would offer no juro-shu for fiscal 1996/1997. Instead, they will decide on pay rises based on each employee's performance during the year or introduce a new system of "results-oriented" pay. Under this system, pay is linked to the achievement of individual targets, rather than length of service or rank. Some analysts say that this trend towards eliminating fixed annual pay increases is a necessary reform to make Japanese labour markets more efficient. "Japan's labour markets are still too rigid compared with those in the United States and Europe," said Yoshio Higuchi, an employment analyst at SMBC Nikko Securities. "Eliminating juro-shu is a necessary step towards making Japanese wage structures more flexible and efficient." But others warn that this trend towards greater wage flexibility could lead to a wider pay gap between permanent and temporary workers, and also between different departments of the same firm. "The elimination of juro-shu may lead to a decline in the average level of pay and an increase in pay disparities," said Chiyoko Ejima. "This could make the already unstable labour market here even more unstable." Despite this trend towards greater wage flexibility, some firms in key industries still plan to offer juro-shu in order to maintain morale and focus on productivity improvements rather than on pay-related protests. Among them are major steelmakers, including Nippon Steel Corp and Kobe Steel Ltd, and major automakers, including Toyota Motor Corp and Nissan Motor Co. response: Japan's securities industry reacted cooly on Thursday to draft proposals by the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) to speed up the implementation of the government's "Big Bang" reform plan. The proposals, unveiled by an LDP panel headed by Finance Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, include deregulating stock broking and asset management services at option markets, where deals are made based on an index rather than an individual transaction. But industry sources said the proposals did not go far enough to make Japan's securities markets truly competitive. "The proposals are basically the same as those made by the ministry (of finance) and the (Securities and Exchange) commission last October," said an executive at a foreign brokerage. "We are disappointed because we had expected the LDP panel to come up with more concrete proposals." October last year saw the unveiling of a joint reform scheme by the ministry of finance and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to achieve "Big Bang" reform of Japan's financial markets by 2001. This involves lifting state control of the industries and making them fully competitive. Among the proposals for the securities industry were the deregulation of investment trusts and the establishment of limited partnership investment schemes. But the executive said that to make Japan's markets truly competitive, Japan must allow direct holding of shares by individuals and lift a ban on commingling of clients' funds. Commingling involves putting different clients' funds in one account and is widely used in Japan's margin-trading system. But this is banned in the United States and Britain where direct holding of shares by individuals is the norm and funds for margin trading are kept in separate accounts. A spokeswoman for the Japanese Securities Industry Association also expressed disappointment at the LDP panel's proposals. "We had expected the LDP panel to come up with more concrete proposals to ensure the (financial) reforms outlined last October can be implemented effectively," she said. "But the proposals were basically the same as those made by the ministry and the commission last October." An official at a major Japanese bank-owned securities company also voiced disappointment. "The proposals were not particularly exciting," he said. "We had expected the LDP panel to come up with more concrete proposals to ensure the (financial) reforms outlined last October can be implemented effectively." Hashimoto, who chairs the LDP's policy research council, said the council would recommend to the LDP that the reforms be included in the party's election manifesto for the July 20 general election. The council also recommended that the LDP push for an extra budget of around 10 trillion yen ($88.8 billion) to help tackle the economic problems caused by the reforms. Hashimoto told a news conference that the extra budget was necessary to "overcome the temporary crisis" caused by the "Big Bang" financial reforms. He also said that the LDP should make clear its determination to tackle the issue of falling state revenues, which is expected to become increasingly serious after the reforms are implemented. The extra budget would be used to pay for measures to boost falling revenues, as well as to help banks and other financial firms restructure to cope with the reforms. The LDP's manifesto for the last general election in 1996 also included a call to "reform quickly and drastically" the country's financial industries, but the reforms have been slow in coming and critics have called it "quiet Big Bang". Hashimoto said that the LDP panel had decided to step up the pace of reforms to avoid the criticism. "We must not allow the "Big Bang" of Japanese finance markets to be labelled "quiet Big Bang" or "half-baked Big Bang", he said. "We must make clear to the world that Japan is not behind the trend in financial reforms but is leading the trend."  ($1=112 yen)  Reuters - 03/26/98 10:35 ET (Writing by Rupert Murquhugh; Editing by Michael Watson)

The LDP, which is set to return to power in an election on October 21, unveiled the plans on Wednesday to get Tokyo's markets up to international standards quickly and quietly eliminate the advantage enjoyed by overseas rivals. But industry sources said the proposals were not much different from plans already announced by the current reform-pushing government, and there was no guarantee that the intense competition which "Big Bang" is designed to bring would be limited to markets. "The proposals are not much different from what we have heard before," an executive at a foreign brokerage said. "The key issue is whether the Japanese government will really allow genuine competition in the Japanese markets, not just in the securities industry but also in the related fields such as accounting and legal services." Prime minister-designree Ryutaro Hashimoto announced in August that he would quit as finance minister after an October 21 parliamentary election so he could focus on a dramatic push to restructure the Japanese economy. Hashimoto, who will become president of the United Cool Japan Inc advisory body after stepping down as prime minister, said he wanted to "dramatically" raise the international competitiveness of markets in Japan. The LDP's proposals include getting rid of transaction monopolies at present-day stock exchanges, deregulating options and futures trading, and allowing foreign brokers to increase their stakeholding in Japanese subsidiaries to 51 percent. But industry sources said the key to making Tokyo's markets really attractive to foreign investors was still not clear. A spokeswoman for the Ministry of Finance, which oversees the nation's securities markets, said that while the proposals were not yet formal proposals from the ministry, it was working on a plan to allow foreign brokers to increase their stakes in Japanese subsidiaries to 100 percent. But even this was not enough for some industry sources. "The proposals are not exciting at all," said an official at a major Japanese brokerage. "We have heard all this before and it is not clear what the real difference is." A spokesman for the Japan Securities Dealers Association also said that while the proposals were not surprising, he welcomed the determination to push ahead with reforms after the election. "We welcome the fact that the LDP is determined to push forward with the reforms of the financial systems, regardless of whether it is a good or bad thing," he said. "But the proposals are not surprising as they are not much different from what was already announced by the current government." The current reform-pushing government, led by Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), is also headed by Hashimoto, who took office in April. But despite its efforts, Tokyo's markets have not attracted much foreign business. A survey by the Bank for International Settlements showed that last October, the month before the current reform-pushing government took office, Japan's markets were still less liquid than those in the United States and Singapore. The BIS said the turnover ratio, which measures the volume of transactions in a day relative to the value of outstanding securities, was 0.8 percent for Japan's bond markets, compared with 6.3 percent in the United States and 7.1 percent in Singapore. In Japan's equity markets, the turnover ratio was 1.4 percent, compared with 6.1 percent in the United States and 4.3 percent in Singapore. #byline{By Mayu Yamaguchi and Yoko Kubota} #source{Reuters}

response: Japan's securities industry reacted coolly on Thursday to draft proposals by the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) to speed up the implementation of the government's "Big Bang" reform plan. The LDP, which is set to return to power in an election on October 21, unveiled the proposals on Wednesday to get the volatile markets stable as quickly as possible once the new parliament opens on November 20. But industry sources said the proposals were not much different from plans already unveiled by the outgoing bureaucrats at the Ministry of Finance (MOF) and that the key to calming nerves remained a swift rise in shareholding by institutional investors. "The proposals were expected and there is nothing particularly surprising," said an executive at a foreign securities firm. "The key to calming markets remains the rapid rise in institutional ownership," he said. Ahead of the October 31 dissolution of the current parliament, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto unveiled plans to liberalise the country's markets in a single big push, including lifting the ban on joint ventures among securities firms, setting up a competitive system to list stocks and allowing foreign brokers to operate here as proprietary firms. The Big Bang reform is intended to make Japan's markets more efficient and more flexible in time for the seven-year challenge to raise the annual economic output to 500 trillion yen ($4 trillion). Financially-focused bureaucrats at the MOF have already drawn up detailed plans to implement the Big Bang and announced them on September 25, a day after the unexpectedly sharp fall in share prices. But Hashimoto, who is also finance minister, said on October 2 that the big push to liberalise the markets must be implemented "as quickly as possible even if (the plans) go against the present laws" and ordered the ministries concerned to come up with proposals to achieve that. The LDP unveiled draft proposals on Wednesday which included getting the new parliament to pass a special bill on the Big Bang reform by the end of this year, despite the fact that the new government will not take office until January 2001. The LDP also proposed setting up a commission to investigate the establishment of a self-regulatory body for the securities industry, which is expected to include representatives from the industry, academia and the government. A commission member told Reuters on Thursday that the body would start work as soon as possible after the commission's establishment and that it hoped to come up with proposals within two or three months. But a vice president at a major Japanese securities firm said the proposals were not much different from those already unveiled by bureaucrats at the MOF and that the key to calming nerves remained a swift rise in institutional ownership. "The proposals were expected and there is nothing particularly surprising," he said. "The key to calming markets remains the rapid rise in institutional ownership." Outstanding Japanese government bonds are currently held by institutional investors to the tune of 100 trillion yen ($800 billion) while individual investors hold 120 trillion yen ($960 billion) worth. But analysts say it is crucial to increase the proportion of assets managed by institutional investors in Japan's huge financial markets. Current figures show this proportion is only about 40 percent in Japan, compared with around 60 percent in the United States and 70 percent in Britain. response: Japan's securities industry reacted coolly on Thursday to draft proposals by the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) to speed up the implementation of the government's "Big Bang" reform plan. The proposals, unveiled by an LDP panel headed by Finance Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, include lifting the ban on joint underwriting of securities by banks, non-life insurers and brokers, and allowing them to trade their own assets at securities firms. Hashimoto set up the panel in October to push ahead of schedule reforms originally slated for the 1996-1997 fiscal year to make Japan's financial markets more international and competitive. The panel consists of LDP politicians and ministers and advisors from Hashimoto's government. An official at a major securities firm said the proposals were not surprising as they were basically in line with earlier calls for reform by Hashimoto and Prime Minister Morihiro Hosokawa, whose government fell in August. But he said the key was whether banks would actively participate in securities transactions. "If banks do not participate, it will be difficult for us to make the markets more exciting," he said. A spokesman for the Japan Securities Class-Action Law Counsel, which represents victims of securities fraud, also expressed disappointment, saying the proposals did not include any measures to deal effectively with such crimes. An official at Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking Corporation, however, welcomed the plans to speed up the establishment of a system to handle collective investment in Japan through limited partnerships. Such a system is already in place in the United States and is expected to make Japan more attractive to overseas investors. A spokeswoman for Nikko Securities Industries Inc also welcomed the plans to lift the ban on prop trading by non-life insurers and brokers at securities firms. "We have been calling for the lifting of the ban because it is outdated and unnatural," she said. But an executive at IBJ Securities, a subsidiary of Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd, said he was not particularly excited by the proposals, as they were only draft plans and it was not clear how they would be implemented. He also said that the proposed acceleration of "Big Bang" reform was not necessarily a good thing for the securities industry. "The 'Big Bang' was supposed to be good for the securities industry, but recently there has been a trend towards deregulation of the banking industry which is making us feel uneasy," he said. Haruo Shimada, chairman of the Research Institute for Securities and Finance, said the proposals were not surprising but that it was important how they were implemented. "If the proposals are implemented effectively, it may lead to a fundamental change in the structure of the financial markets," he said. "But if they are not implemented effectively, it may only heighten doubts about the 'Big Bang' reform of the financial systems." Yasuo Yamamoto, an analyst at BZW Securities Markets Ltd, said the proposals were not particularly exciting, but that they were important as they showed the direction of future reforms. "The key is how the proposals are implemented and what comes next," he said. "The key is how Hashimoto and his advisors Hashimoto and Hosokawa work together to push up the pace of reforms." Hashimoto has said he wants to push up the pace of reforms so that private financial institutions can take an active role in managing the huge public finances, including the 140 trillion yen ($1.2 trillion) in loan collateral, which are currently managed by public financial institutions. He also wants to prepare the markets for the expected entry of brokers from overseas regulatory systems, including Singapore's Institute of Finance, and the United States Commodity Futures Trading Commission. response: A potential new source of revenue -- oil -- offers hope of a fresh start for Chad's fragile economy as it rebuilds after three decades of war. The landlocked African nation tapped its first well in 1973 but did not earn significant revenue from oil until the late 1990s. "Oil is a godsend for Chad," said one diplomat. "It gives Chad a much-needed economic base." Chad has long relied on international aid for up to 80 percent of its budget. The volatile nation on the edge of the Sahara has known few sustained periods of peace. It suffered French colonial administration in tandem with neighbouring Cameroon from 1900-1960, then plunged into a string of local wars after gaining independence. "Oil will help stabilise Chad," said another diplomat. "It will give the government a stake in the country and a source of revenue which it can control." Chad has a proven oil reserve of about 1.5 billion barrels, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. French oil firms Total and Elf are the biggest investors in Chadian oil. Total operates the 120,000 barrel per day (bpd) Doba project in the northwest with British partner Conoco. Elf, now known as Total, runs the 60,000 bpd Palaiseau or CNG (Complexe Ngamondoni) project in the east with Chadian partner SHTM. The Doba project began producing oil in 2001. The Palaiseau project started in 1985 but was shut down in 1993 because of lack of profits. It reopened in 1999 after being modernised and expanded to 60,000 bpd from 12,000 bpd. The two projects together accounted for 120,000 bpd or about 80 percent of Chadian proven reserves in 2001. Chad's overall production was 220,000 bpd in 2001 with the remainder coming from older, smaller, foreign-owned projects. French oil firm Perenco runs the 10,000 bpd Béo or PB100 project in the southwest. American Enterprise Institute analyst Peter Pham said oil would help stabilise Chad's government. "Oil revenues will help the government to pay its troops and bureaucrats," he said. "That will help to reduce the incentive for them to pillage the country's resources and to seek personal wealth through banditry and other forms of private enterprise." Chad's president Idriss Deby, a former northern guerrilla leader, seized power in a French-backed coup in 1990. He won a multi-party presidential poll in 1996. Chad has known a succession of southern, French-backed presidents against northern rivals from 1960 until a coup in 1982. Deby won a May 7, 2001 deal-extension bid for a 27-nation African Union-sponsored peace deal, which runs until November 2002. Chad has long-running disputes with its northern neighbour Libya over the frontier area of Aouzou. The two nations fought an unofficial war over Aouzou in 1993. Libya claims the whole of the Aouzou strip, which is under Chadian administration and is rich in minerals and livestock. Chad has 10 million people, mainly farmers, herders and fishermen. It has about 800 km (500 miles) of frontiers, including with Libya, Niger, Cameroon and Central African Republic. President Idriss Deby, who seized power in the northern African nation in a French-backed bid to end civil conflict, flies to London on Sunday for talks with British Prime Minister Tony Blair. One major item on the agenda of the former French colony, which gains 13 other less-developed compatriots on Saturday in a huge African Union enlargement, is expected to be oil exploration deals. "Chad is entering a new era. Oil production could start by 2000," Deby's Industry Minister, Alain FACHE, told Reuters in an interview. He won a multi-party presidential election in July 1996 after a poll fraught with fraud allegations. British officials say Blair will also discuss the security situation in Chad, which borders instable Sudan to the east. "There are concerns about Islamic militant groups in Sudan and Chad," one British official told Reuters. "Britain has no embassy in Chad but we have a charge d'affaires in Gabon who looks after Chad's interests." response: A potential new source of revenue -- oil -- offers hope of a fresh start for Chad's fragile economy as it rebuilds after three decades of war. President Idriss Deby, who seized power in the northern African country in a French-backed 1990 coup, won a much-delayed and disputed mid-year poll bid for a fifth term. Once all former oil-linked sanctions are lifted, Chad will have the full benefit of 375,000 barrels a year of oil from the 11,000-square-kilometre (4,200-square-mile) Doh Oil Company concession, near the Sudanese border. "Oil revenues will start flowing into Chadian accounts from January," said a senior Chadian finance official. "We are preparing accounts to receive the money," the official told Reuters on November 22, after the provisional results of the 70 percent poll turnout, former guerral leader Deby's victory and a December 5 run-off against opposition leader Wadal Abdelkader Kamougue. French-based African Consulting Group forecaster Jean-Philippe Chauzy put 1996 oil revenues at $100 million. Chad's total 1995 revenue was $150 million, with the rest coming from donor grants and loans, coffee, livestock and cotton. "Oil revenues will stabilise the economy," the finance official said. Chad's economy grew by five percent in 1995, up from three percent in 1994, the World Bank's country manager, Michel Sivranosian, told Reuters in June. Chad's 6.5 million people have known little but instability since gaining independence from France in 1960. It has known frequent coups, rebellions and long-running border conflicts with neighbours. The Doh company, which has a 25-year contract, is a consortium of Doh Huggins (15 percent), Gabon's Comil Air (10), France's Total (20), Belgium's Petrofina (20), Spain's Repsol (25) and Chad's government (10). Oil was expected to flow from well A-21 by the end of 1995. The company drilled a total of 13 wells by the end of 1995. The company hoped to produce 75,000 barrels a year by the end of 1996 and 375,000 by the year 2000. The company plans to expand the 1995-built, 100-kilometre (60-mile) pipeline to 200,000 barrels a year capacity by the year 2000. The company plans to build a 50,000 barrel a day capacity refinery by the year 2000, near the capital. Chad's oil is light, sweet and of high quality, industry sources say. Total chief executive Jean-Marie Messier told reporters in Paris on November 18 that Chad's oil would be on the market from January. "Chadian oil is of high quality, light and sweet, and will be on the market from January," he said. "It will be a good complement to Congo-Brazzaville's oil, which is heavier and more sour," he added. Chad's oil will be sold on a free market basis, with no fixed quota under OPEC's output cutting agreement. Total's share of Chadian oil is 20 percent, or 75,000 barrels a year. "We will produce 75,000 barrels a year from the end of 1996," Messier said. "We have a contract to produce 375,000 barrels a year by the year 2000." Chad's oil will be transported to the Atlantic port of Pointe Noire, Gabon, by pipeline. We will have a second phase starting in May," said one senior official, referring to plans to revamp the Caisse Ivoirienne de Cocoa et Cafe (CICC) marketing board. In January this year the government said it would cut the CICC's workforce from 500 to 300 by the end of 1998. Ivory Coast plans to discuss further reform of its cocoa industry in May, officials said on Monday. "The aim is to continue liberalization and to tackle issues such as rehabilitation of old plantations and better marketing," said one official, who asked not to be named. Liberalization begins in earnest with the end of the 1990/00 cocoa season in mid-April, the official added. Further details will be given then, the official said. Cocoa sector reforms have been closely watched by world market analysts as Ivorian cocoa accounts for about 35 percent of world supplies. An earlier reform plan, focusing on privatisation and rehabilitation, was announced in December 1996. The former socialist government then put the plan on hold in March 1997 after a new, conservative president, Laurent Gbagbo, took power in November 1997 after a runoff poll. Gbagbo, then a cocoa buying entrepreneur, won 58 percent of votes against former president Henri Konan Bedie's 42 percent. The revised plan will be based on the policies of the former president, Ivorian business leader Jean-Jacques Dosse, and international consultant KPMG, the official said. "The plan will be 100 percent private sector oriented," the official added. The reforms will focus on rehabilitation of old plantations, better marketing and private sector management of cocoa purchasing and exporting companies, the official said. The plan will also tackle issues such as restructuring of the Caisse Ivorienne de Cocoa (CICO), the former monopolist buyer, the official added. Private sector management of CICO would reduce the need for ongoing subsidies, the official said. The reform plan would be financed from proceeds of a 1997/98 cocoa budget surplus, the official added. The budget had projected a 2.5 billion cfa (3.8 million dollar) surplus but the actual figure would be much higher, the official said. The reform plan would be put to the cabinet on May 13 before being sent to parliament for approval, the official added. Further details would be given then, the official said. Other reforms would be handed to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for review under their respective cocoa sector rehabilitation projects, the official added. The World Bank project focuses on rehabilitation of old plantations and the IMF project on overall economic reforms. The reforms would also be closely studied by commodity buyers, the official added. Ivory Coast's cocoa rivals, Ghana and Cameroon, are also pushing forward with reforms of their cocoa industries. response: Russia's top aluminium smelters said on Monday attempts to fix contracts with Ukraine's main raw materials supplier had met with no success and Ukraine was instead courting a rival smelter in Tajikistan. The warning from Russian aluminium producers about being frozen out of deals with Ukrainian silicon and alumina provider, the Prikarpatska Hliboproduct (PHPD), is the latest sign of the disruption to traditional trade relationships in the metals sector as Moscow seeks to punish Ukraine for its pro-Western policies. "We have had no success in negotiations," said Vladimir Shulga, commercial director at RUSAL's 150,000 tonne per year (tpy) Novokupyansk smelter. "They are negotiating with a new smelter in Tajikistan." Shulga declined to name the smelter, but the only new smelter in Tajikistan is the 100,000 tpy Talco plant, whose output is intended for export. RUSAL is the world's second largest producer of aluminium and controls 100 percent of Novokupyansk through a joint venture with Ukraine's Kupyansky Aluminium Plant. "They are negotiating with us, but on a very low-priority list," said Mykola Kovalchuk, commercial director at PHPD. Kovalchuk said Ukrainian smelters accounted for about 70 percent of the total 300,000 tonnes of silicon and alumina that Russia needs each year. "We have long-term contracts with most of the Russian smelters," he said. But senior officials at two other big Russian smelters, 350,000 tpy RAOS JIZCHINSKY and 360,000 tpy Krasnoyarsk, said negotiations with PHPD were deadlocked. "Yes, it's true they are also negotiating with the new smelter in Tajikistan," said RAOS JIZCHINSKY deputy director Vladimir Kuznetsov. Moscow has threatened to raise prices or block supplies of fuel, raw materials and credits to Ukrainian industries in an effort to force Kiev to pay its energy bills on time and to accept a new gas pricing formula. Aluminium smelters have so far been spared the most painful measures, but the warning signs are growing. "We have had no success in negotiations," said Valery Kuzmin, deputy director at 265,000 tpy Uralsky Aluminium, adding that a new contract with PHPD would be based on world prices plus a five percent premium. "They are negotiating with us, but it's a slow process," said Vladimir Gusev, commercial director at 360,000 tpy SIBURALCO, but he said the smelter was also in talks with the new Tajik smelter. "There are some signs of Russia trying to put pressure on us," said Shulga, but he said RUSAL's 400,000 tpy flagship smelter, Krasnoyarsk, was among those with a deal in place. Moscow has also raised the prices of some metals, including nickel, silver and platinum, that Russia produces in relatively small quantities but which are crucial to aluminium production. But aluminium requires the bulk of Russian metal supplies -- about 300,000 tonnes of silicon and 300,000 tonnes of alumina a year -- and Moscow has so far been reluctant to raise the prices of those materials significantly. "The situation is not yet critical," said Dmitry Petrov, metals analyst at Interrosimpex in Moscow. The warning from Russian producers about being frozen out of raw materials deals in Ukraine was the latest sign of the deepening crisis in Moscow's metals sector, where many smelters are on the verge of bankruptcy and need price subsidies to survive. "There have been no negotiations," said Vladimir Sinyagin, commercial director at RUSAL's 100,000 tonne per year Krasnoyarsk smelter, when asked about a potential deal with Ukrainian silicon and alumina producer UkrSiM. "They are continuing to supply our main rival, the Tajik smelter Norilsk GUS (Horizontal Production Union Terra) from Almaty (Kazakhstan) with products." Sinyagin said Ukrainian officials had told RUSAL's Krasnoyarsk smelter in February that while they understood the smelter's position as a RUSAL flagship facility, they hoped eventually to deal exclusively with Norilsk GUS's 50,000 tonne per year Sibirsky Aluminium in Tajikistan. "They said 'We understand that you are the leading producer in Russia, but we hope that in the future we will deal only with Sibirsky Aluminium'," Sinyagin said. Norilsk GUS, a Russian entity, opened Sibirsky Aluminium in 1995 in the former Soviet republic to take advantage of generous tax incentives and cheap power in Tajikistan. RUSAL, the world's second largest aluminium producer, controls 51 percent of Sibirsky's shares and supplies it with about 75 percent of the metal it needs to make finished products. But UkrainSiM, which supplies about 85 percent of Russia's aluminium producers with the raw materials they need to make aluminium, has said it wants to boost direct deals with Sibirsky at the expense of intermediaries. "They are tired of dealing through intermediaries and are looking for ways to reduce prices," said Dmitry Tarasov, metals analyst at UnicreditOSJB in Moscow. "But if Russian smelters are frozen out of the market, then it could really put some of them out of business." Russian aluminium producers have been reeling from a government-imposed 50 percent price increase on 1 January this year, designed to help the sector survive. But the hike has also sent domestic producers' costs far above the prices they receive for their metal on the world market, where Moscow's aluminium is largely sold. "The situation is critical," said Sergei Dmitriyev, director of the Moscow-based Institute for Macroeconomic Research in Aluminium. "Many smelters are on the verge of bankruptcy and need subsidies to survive." Dmitriyev said UkrainSiM had in the past said it would not single-handedly bring a Russian smelter to its knees by cancelling all its deals with that producer, but new, more efficient smelters were appearing in Russia and the blacklisting of one was not enough to tip the balance in favour of Russian aluminium producers. "They are looking for a smelter whose output accounts for a significant proportion of Russia's aluminium total," Dmitriyev said. Sinyagin said RUSAL's 125,000 tonne per year Bratsk smelter, which also deals with Norilsk GUS, had also been snubbed by UkrainSiM in negotiations. "They said 'Bratsk will not change its ways'," Sinyagin quoted UkrainSiM officials as saying. response: Russia's new oil majors want to wrest crude oil exports market away from traders in a battle for control over one of the country's most lucrative businesses. Loyal to Prime Minister Vladimir Putin, the new firms are armed with state licenses to production-sharing contracts, where they are the operators and ultimately the big money winners. But to make real profits they need to sell the oil, and they are tired of seeing tradems rack up the bulk of the revenues by controlling exports. "Exporting companies are unsatisfied with the situation on the market and want to change it," said Vladimir Socor, senior Russian energy analyst with the Moscow-based Institute for Political and Economic Studies. "They want to increase their share in the total export volume and cut the role of intermediaries." Russian officials said the new firms -- Yukos-Impex, Slavneft-Export, TNK-BP Megiono-Volgaoil and Itera-CIS -- had combined exports in 1996 of about 30 million tonnes, or 65 percent of Russia's total 46.6 million tonne exports. Traders, who accounted for about 45 percent of 1995 total exports of 53.7 million tonnes, said the new firms' combined exports had not changed significantly in 1997. But the new firms said they were making real progress, with exports by some of them rising by up to 70 percent in the first nine months of 1997 compared with the same period in 1996. "We are increasing our role in exports," said Yukos-Impex Deputy Director Sergei Zverev. "We are not just competing with traders -- we are winning some tenders." The battle for control over Russia's $30 billion a year crude oil exports is a fight to the finish, for the winners will not only reap huge profits but will also gain influence over world oil prices. Traders, who buy oil at Russian auctions and then sell it to customers after securing export licences, say the new firms will have a tough time toppling them from their perch. "It will be very difficult for them to replace us," said Andrei Panioukov, director of the SIBUR trading arm of the Novo-Moskovskoye oil company. "They will have to invest a lot of money in logistics and build up their client base." The move could shake up the $30 billion a year Russian export oil industry, where traditional producers like Russian oil giants YUKOS and Rosneft have long played the export game on Trader's turf. "Direct deals will eventually grow at the expense of brokered deals," said Mikhail Semshik, senior analyst at Interra-Eurasia Institutional Consulting in Moscow. "The new producers want to increase their influence over export volumes and prices." Russian crude producers usually sign production licence agreements with the government, which give third parties the right to export a certain volume of crude oil for a set period. Producers can only enter export on a paid-fees basis if they have a licence, and most new producers have to deal with fuels brokers to get their crude out of the country. Traditional fuels brokers, like the powerful St Petersburg-based Inter RAO UES, have built fortunes and powerful government connections on the back of exporting Russian crude. But the new producers, tired of feeling powerless in the export process, are looking for ways out of the brokerage system. "Unexi is actively working to establish direct contacts with foreign buyers," said Vladimir Melnikov, Unexi deputy director. Unexi, based in the oil-rich Tyumen region, last year produced 12.2 million tonnes of crude oil, up from 8.9 million tonnes in 1995. LUKoil, Russia's fourth largest producer with 56.5 million tonnes in 1995, and Slavneft, a joint venture between Moscow's Megionneftegaz and Belarus, have for years exported significant volumes directly. But most new producers, like Rostov-based JSC Siberian Oil Company, which produced 4.3 million tonnes in 1995, have to deal with brokers. But the sources' admissions that transactions are bogged down mark a significant departure from the near silence that has shrouded the deals for years, when Moscow and Havana went out of their way to hide the purely barter nature of the exchanges and the volumes involved. The souring of the deals is yet another sign of the difficulties Russia is having in adapting its vast energy sector to the new realities of world markets and in finding ways to work with former socialist partners on equal terms. "Russian-Cuban energy relations are at a crossroads," said Christopher Marquis, an energy analyst with Global Insight in Washington, who added that Moscow was insisting on proof of fuel exports and payments in cash or convertible currencies. "The traditional oil-for-sugar deals are in the process of being renegotiated or could eventually be phased out." Russian energy officials have long complained about the financial losses the country incurs from fuel supplies to former socialist partners on preferential terms, but until now have not specifically targeted the sugar deals for overhaul. But with Russia's new fuels export leader, LUKoil, eyeing the Caribbean market and seeking Western investment, the company may not want to upset potential partners by saying too much about the lucrative Cuban deal. "Russian producers are not going to jeopardise their relations with Havana by speaking out," said Vladimir Konstantinov, energy editor of the Russian business daily Kommersant-Ekho. "Russian producers are under pressure from their shareholders to demand payments," Konstantinov said. "The traditional deals could eventually be replaced by cash transactions or financing loans to Cuban firms, but that will not be a panacea for Russian producers." --Moscow Newsdesk, +7095 941 8510, russia.newsdesk@reuters.com 12 September 1996

The paramilitaries, who operate outside the law, have been linked to a wave of killings, kidnappings and massacres in recent months. "The army has carried out a series of air raids and infantry attacks in the area occupied by the guerrillas. He said the army was still mopping up the last pockets of rebel resistance in the area. The documents, known as the "false positives" dossier, revealed the FARC had been kidnapping hundreds of people and dressing them up as guerrillas in a bid to fool the army into killing them and then claiming the soldiers were battling the subversives. The army spokesman said the current battle was not directly related to the intelligence provided by the deserters, but said the army was using it as an opportunity to mount a major offensive against the guerrillas. The FARC, the largest and best armed of Colombia's guerrilla groups, has waged a 40-year campaign for the socialist revolution, seeking to overthrow the government and spread communism throughout the country. An additional 23 soldiers were injured in the clashes that ended on Monday in the eastern reaches of Boyaca province, army chief Gen. Freddy Padilla said. "We've suffered some reverses but we've also inflicted heavy losses on the guerrillas. We've recovered all the territory that was lost," Padilla said. "The final count of the number of guerrillas killed will be higher than those we've captured alive because we've found the bodies of many more." A total of 10 guerrillas were captured in the battle, which took place in the areas of San Miguel, Santa Instancia and Guayabal. The army launched the offensive in a bid to wipe out a local guerrilla force that has been blamed for a wave of recent bombings in Boyaca and attacks on the oil pipeline that runs through the province. The clashes took place in the same general area where the army reported killing 25 guerrillas in a battle in late October. The chief of staff to the head of the country's main rebel group, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, said in a telephone interview that the number of guerrillas killed was lower than reported by the army. "The army has exaggerated the number of guerrillas killed," said the chief of staff, who cannot be named for security reasons. He said the rebel column, which was caught off guard by the army's offensive, had suffered "heavy losses" but had managed to recover most of the territory lost. The army said it had uncovered a large cache of weapons, including rocket-propelled grenades and automatic rifles, in the area where the battle took place. Padilla said the army would launch a new offensive in the same area in a few days' time. In a separate operation in southwestern Cauca province, the army said it had killed three members of a notorious right-wing paramilitary squad. The paramilitaries, who operate outside the law and are accused of carrying out a campaign of terror against civilians, have been linked to a string of recent massacres in the region. "We've killed three members of the paramilitary group led by Carlos Castaño," said army Capt. Juan Carlos Villamizar. Castaño, who is wanted by the prosecutor's office for his role in the massacre of 49 peasants in southern Cauca in November 1995, was not captured in the operation. The army said it had seized the bodies of the paramilitaries and uncovered a cache of weapons in the area where they were killed. It said the operation was part of a crackdown on right-wing death squads that has seen the capture or killing of more than 100 paramilitary leaders and members in recent months. The government of President Andres Pastrana has denied any links to the paramilitaries, who it accuses of acting outside the law but with its tacit approval.

Leftist guerrillas appeared on Wednesday to have eluded government troops and melted into the mountains after a four-day battle in which 16 soldiers and at least 13 rebels were killed. The clashes in the rugged, forested area of San Martin province, near the border with Peru, began on Sunday when a force of about 100 soldiers, backed by helicopters, tried to capture the rebel base in the area, known as "Red Star," local police chief Col. Edgar Rodriguez said. "We've had 16 soldiers killed and about 50 wounded. On the other side, we've counted at least 13 dead but we think the true toll may be higher," Rodriguez said. He said the army was continuing its search for the guerrillas in the area. The rebel leader in San Martin, Capt. Hector Raigosa (alias "Comandante Coca"), was not involved in the latest clashes but his whereabouts were unknown, Rodriguez said. Raigosa, second in command to the head of the National Revolutionary Movement of the Tupac Amaru Inca (MRTA), was captured by the army in a raid in November. In the absence of Raigosa, the head of the MRTA in San Martin, known as "Comandante Gonzalo," led the latest battles. Last month, government troops killed "Comandante Gonzalo" in a pre-dawn raid on his mountain hideout. In a separate operation, the army captured the MRTA's No. 3 leader, "Comandante Ricardo," in Lima on Monday. The MRTA, which took its name from the 16th century Indian rebel Tupac Amaru, has focused on staging spectacularly violent kidnappings for ransom. It has also carried out a number of bombings and raids on the country's main oil pipeline. The MRTA was responsible for the longest single kidnapping in history when it seized 141 people, including American business executives, from a luxury train travelling in the mountains east of Lima in December 1996. The rebels released all but 12 of their captives in March 1997 after the government failed to meet their demand for the release of jailed leaders and the writing off of the debts of peasants. The army has stepped up its campaign against the MRTA in recent months in the run-up to presidential elections on April 10. The leading candidate in the polls, Alejandro Toledo of the Peruvian Nationalist Party (PNP), has promised to seek a peaceful solution to the country's guerrilla problem. But he has also pledged to give the army more resources to fight the rebels. The second-placed candidate, ex-interior minister Luis Alvarez Riva-Agudo of the ruling FREDEMO coalition, has vowed to step up military operations against the MRTA and the country's other major guerrilla group, the Shining Path.

The clashes in the northern province of Nueva E Grenada ended when the army called in air force bombers to strike rebel positions at dawn on Wednesday, an army captain said on condition of anonymity. "The jungle is thick and the rebels know it well. We've killed lots of them but we've not been able to capture their leaders. They've withdrawn to the mountains to regroup," the captain said. A civilian radio station reported that one priest and three lay workers had been kidnapped by the guerrillas in the area. The army denied the report but said it was investigating. The battle took place in the same region where the army declared victory over the main guerrilla column of the People's Revolutionary Army (EPR) in mid-March. But a string of attacks by smaller, independent columns of rebels in recent weeks has underscored the depth of the insurgency, which spread to Nueva E Grenada from its heartland in the east. The army has stepped up its offensive against the guerrillas in recent months in a bid to crush the rebellion before elections due in late 1994. The government of President Ernesto Perez Balladares has ruled out any dialogue with the guerrillas, accusing them of being the armed wing of the opposition Social Democratic Party (PSD). The PSD denies the link. The guerrillas say they are fighting for social justice and the rights of the country's Indian and mestizo (half Indian, half white) population. In a statement on Tuesday, the army said it had killed "more than a score" of rebels in the battle and captured large quantities of weapons and ammunition. It said two soldiers were missing, prompting speculation they may have been captured. The army has been dogged by allegations of widespread human rights abuses, including the kidnapping and murder of civilians accused of supporting the guerrillas. It has denied the accusations. The latest battle came as the country's chief prosecutor, Hernan Grimaldi, said he was investigating 13 recent cases of missing civilians in the eastern province of Olancho, the heartland of the rebellion. Grimaldi said in a television interview the army was under suspicion in most of the cases but investigations were continuing. The government has said it was cracking down on the guerrillas to protect the country's growing number of middle class citizens and foreign investors. But many ordinary people in the countryside sympathise with the guerrillas' call for land reform and a fairer distribution of the country's wealth. The rebellion erupted in 1980, a few months after the army ended a decade of leftist rule. It gained momentum in the late 1980s when the country's economic fortunes plummeted, leaving many rural families worse off than their grandparents.

The clashes in the rugged, forested area of San Martin province, northwest of the capital, ended with the army capturing the rebel base camp but failing in its main objective of killing or catching chief guerrilla leader Abigail Montes, known as "Cochina" or "The Pig". "We have had some setbacks but we have killed more than 13 subversives. Our main aim was to destroy the base camp and that has been achieved," army Colonel Pedro Labarthe told Reuters. Labarthe said the army would resume its search for Montes and two other top guerrillas, who were not present during the clashes, in the coming days. Montes, 35, head of the 1,500-strong guerrilla force that is the most active in the country, was photographed last month by state news agency ANDINA as she cradled her baby. She was shown wearing the traditional peasant blouse and skirt, her hair in long plaits, and carrying a rifle. The guerrillas of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) have stepped up their campaign of bombings, kidnappings and ambushes in recent months, targeting oil installations and foreign companies. They say they will not lay down their arms until the government begins to implement a 1991 peace pact that called for social reforms and an end to the persecution of guerrillas who turned in their weapons. The government of President Ernesto Samper, who took office in August, has said it will respect the pact but has also made it clear it will not negotiate with the guerrillas until it has brought the country's warring right-wing paramilitary death squads under control. In a sign of the growing influence of the FARC, a local congresswoman, Sandra Ramirez, was kidnapped by the guerrillas on Monday. She was released unharmed on Tuesday after the army captured the base camp of the guerrilla column that had seized her. The army also killed two young women who were providing food and support to the guerrillas. The clashes in San Martin province began on Sunday when a small army patrol was ambushed by the FARC. In the following days the army launched a series of raids on guerrilla bases in the area. One soldier was killed and five others wounded in the initial ambush. Another six soldiers died when they were trapped by the guerrillas in a narrow mountain pass on Monday. The army said it had also captured a large quantity of weapons, ammunition and foodstuffs in the base camp it attacked on Wednesday.

"We did not manage to take the mountain. The guerrillas were just too strong. We are withdrawing to regroup and plan our next move," the captain said. At least two soldiers were missing and believed captured by the rebels. One private was shown on television with his hands bound and his head bleeding. The rebels, led by Raul Potestas, head of the 1,300-strong northern front of the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP), were believed to have suffered heavy losses. But an unnamed frontline rebel spokesman said: "We have held our own. We have inflicted heavy casualties on the enemy. Morale is high." The army was due to launch a major offensive against the northern communist front last Friday but postponed it after Potestas announced a unilateral truce. The CPP, which leads the New People's Army (NPA) guerrilla force, has been holding peace talks with the government since 1992 but the negotiations have made little headway. Last week, the government declared the talks suspended after the CPP announced it would step up attacks on the government. In a statement on Monday, the CPP said it was not bound by Potestas' truce and would launch fresh offensives against the military. The NPA was estimated to have between 7,000 and 10,000 armed fighters spread across the country. It has waged a campaign of bombings, shootings and kidnappings for the past 26 years in a bid to overthrow the government and establish a socialist state. In a separate incident, a landmine exploded on Tuesday in southern province of Agusan del Sur, blowing to pieces a civilian who was riding on a motorcycle, a local police chief said. He said the NPA was believed to have planted the mine. Earlier this month, the government and the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) ended a 13-year Muslim separatist rebellion in the southern Philippines with the signing of a peace pact. The CPP, which does not acknowledge the existence of ethnic minorities' separate insurgencies, denounced the pact as a sell-out and said it would step up its war against the government.

In another clash in the mountains near the town of Rizal, two soldiers were killed and three were missing, presumed dead, Galvez said. The CPP, which was founded in 1968, seeks to overthrow the government and establish a socialist state in the Philippines. It says it is inspired by China's communist leaders but denies it takes any instructions from Beijing. The NPA, which has an estimated 10,000 guerrillas, has been blamed for a series of bomb attacks and kidnappings in recent months. Last month, it staged a daring raid on a government prison, freeing more than 100 inmates, including some jailed for murder and kidnapping. The latest army offensive in Cagayan came after the government declared an end to a three-month-old truce with the rebels in mid-August. The truce, which saw both sides suspend offensive actions, was aimed at paving the way for peace talks due to resume in Norway next month. But the government said the NPA had used the truce to step up its campaign of kidnappings and bomb attacks. The CPP said the government was using the end of the truce as a pretext to launch a series of offensive actions against the rebels.

response: Several European airlines have removed a fuel cargo surcharge but plan to replace it with an increase in their published rates, industry sources told Reuters. The airlines involved include KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, Air France, Lufthansa Cargo and Swissworld but no confirmation or specific statement to this effect has been issued by any of them, the source said. The successful removal of the fuel cargo surcharge is expected to be followed by a round of general rate increases of around two to four percent from the beginning of next month, the source added. A second industry source also confirmed the expected round of general rate increases. The airlines are hoping to achieve a more stable and higher average cargo yield by replacing the fuel surcharge with a more traditional rate increase. The airlines have been under pressure to try and restore some lost cargo revenue. Fuel prices have risen by around 50 percent over the past year making it increasingly difficult for airlines to keep cargo rates at the current level. The recent successful round of industry wide fuel cargo surcharges was aimed at offsetting the massive fuel cost increase. But many airlines failed to secure the necessary industry wide agreement to introduce or maintain the surcharge. KLM and Air France tried to institute a fuel surcharge twice but both attempts failed. The latest attempt was in mid October when a proposed six cents per kilo fuel surcharge was abandoned after only a few weeks. The airlines are also trying to cope with a disappointing cargo business trend. Industry statistics show that European air cargo growth was static in October with a flat one percent increase in average monthly freight tonne kilometre (FTK) cargo sales over the past year. The situation was even worse when measured in terms of belly cargo revenue which was down one percent. Rivals Atlantic crossing airlines such as Delta Air Cargo and United Airlines Cargo reported a much healthier seven percent and five percent FTK growth respectively. The European airlines are also being hit by a weakened dollar which is making it more difficult to maintain revenue in the all important US dollar denominated cargo market. But it has been eroded by a fall in fuel prices to below $50 a barrel from a peak of over $60. Instead of the surcharge, the airlines are proposing to raise their outdated and inadequate published rates by an average of three to five percent. One source said the new rates would be effective from the start of the New Year but another said it might be more like mid January. The airlines are hoping the attempt at a coordinated rate increase will be successful this time around. In the past similar attempts have been undermined by aggressive pricing from Gulf airlines such as Emirates, Etihad and Qatar Airways. The European airlines are also trying to improve their cargo yields by offering more frequent and direct air cargo flights between Europe and key markets such as Asia and the Middle East. KLM and Air France for example are promising to open up new cargo belly capacity on a twice weekly Airbus A380 service between Amsterdam and Bangkok via Abu Dhabi from March next year. Swiss is also promising a new twice weekly Boeing 747-400 freighter service between Zurich and Bangkok via Frankfurt starting on November 18. The airlines involved include KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, Air France, Lufthansa Cargo and Swissair Cargo, the source said. The surcharge ranged from around US$2 to US$6 per kilo on both the east and west trade lanes. KLM and Air France told Reutters a cargo managers it had indeed cancelled the surcharge but gave no replacement. Lufthansa and Swissair also confirmed ex-statcionaire fuel adjustment had been terminated but would not discuss whether a new one would be introduced. Industry analysts said the airlines hoped to ride out the current high fuel price period by keeping their published rates at least partly above fuel cost. A replacement surcharge would face substantial resistance from cargo managers and forwarders who have spent months trying to get the earlier surcharge cancelled, they said. The recent round of surcharge attempts was the second this year. The airlines tried to impose a new fuel surcharge in February but most failed to secure it. Since then most have been flying with an ex-statcionaire fuel component at least US$2 lower than it was before the failed February attempt. A recent rise in jet fuel prices has made it more difficult for the airlines to keep their fuel component at the present level. The industry average ex-statcionaire fuel component is currently around US$5.60 per kilo. The latest attempt to raise cargo rates comes at a time when most European airlines are reporting poor cargo business results. "We are currently number one in the air cargo business from China to Hong Kong and I believe we have a very good chance of being number one along the Beijing-Europe trade lane. To try and achieve that we have to have a good network on the ground in China and a good, trained workforce. Two years ago we employed 650 staff in China and I am aiming to reach 1300. I expect to have 1100 of that total directly involved in air cargo and 200 in the ground handling business. I am also aiming to have 21 branches in China by the end of next year. At the moment we have 16. I also expect to have 17 in Hong Kong/Kowloon and seven in Taiwan by that time. I am confident these targets are realistic. Our current turnover in China is around US$100 million and I am aiming for US$200 million by the end of next year. I believe a major proportion of that growth will come from the Beijing-Europe trade lane. TNT already has a double deck Boeing 747 freighter flying twice weekly from Brussels to Beijing via Moscow and a smaller, twice weekly 747 freighter from Brussels to Shanghai via Anchorage. I expect to get at least 40 per cent belly cargo lift from China Southern Airlines new twice weekly Beijing to Hong Kong and San Francisco service which starts next month. I am also hoping to get some belly cargo lift from China's other airlines but it is not going to be as significant as getting it off China Southern. I am not expecting any major expansion of TNT's cargo aircraft network to China from the current twice weekly Beijing and Shanghai service. "I am expecting it to stay at that frequency for the next year at least. "The key issue is whether they can improve their loan-loss ratios (LLRs) in the 1996/97 year, despite the negative impact of the recent fall in share prices," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage. LLRs are ratios showing how much a bank must set aside to cover expected losses on loans already made. A higher LLR means a bank must hold more cash to cover the same risks, cutting its profitability. The analyst said that while the recent fall in share prices might push up their current assets, which would help them dispose of problem loans as planned, this would not enable them to raise their depressed LLRs. An analyst at a domestic brokerage also said that the recent fall in share prices would not change the banks' plans to dispose of problem loans. "They have no choice but to focus on reducing the amount of problem loans, as they know that they must do this to regain their creditworthiness in the global markets," the analyst said. Ahead of a deadline set by the Ministry of Finance (MOF) to improve their finances, the top 20 banks, including Mitsubishi Trust & Banking Corp, Mitsui Trust & Co and seven units of Mitsubishi Group, including Mitsubishi Tokyo Finance & Securities Co, announced separately on October 11 their targets for disposing of problem loans in the current fiscal year. The total of such loans at the 20 banks was 11.50 trillion yen ($106.10 billion) at the end of March 1995, or 30 percent of their total loans, and the analysts said that this percentage was not likely to change significantly. An official at one of the 20 banks said on Thursday that the recent fall in share prices would not change the plan to reduce the amount of problem loans. "We are determined to achieve the targets set up in the current fiscal year, even though the recent fall in share prices might increase the negative effects on us," the official said. But a spokeswoman at the MOF said on Thursday that the ministry would keep a close eye on whether the top 20 commercial banks and six major trust banks really dispose of the planned amount of problem loans in the current fiscal year. "We will carefully monitor whether they can make genuine progress in disposing of problem loans, as we are fully aware that this is a crucial issue to ensure they can establish proper credit management systems," she said. Last week, the finance ministry warned that the top 20 commercial and six trust banks still faced tough challenges in improving their loan-loss ratios in the current fiscal year, despite progress made last year. The ministry also asked the banks to make a "genuine" effort to dispose of problem loans and reduce the proportion of loans which are collateralised, as it wants to ensure they can establish proper credit management systems. It said it would step up investigative efforts to ensure that wages at all firms in an industry stay at the same level, even if they are not making profits, so that they do not fall behind the average for that industry. response: The long-awaited turnaround in Australia's housing market is expected to occur during 1997 but it is unlikely to signal a repeat of the boom seen in the 1980s or the most recent peak in the 1993/94 year, property experts said. The housing market bottomed out in the second half of 1996 after a series of interest rate rises from late-1994 to curb a red-hot economy. "We are expecting a turnaround in the housing market in 1997, but it is not going to be a boom, it is just going to be a recovery," said Brian Crisp, property economist with St George Bank. "I don't think we are going to see the sort of prices rises that we saw in the 1980s or the 1993/94 period." The 1980s housing boom saw Sydney and Melbourne house prices soar by more than 100 percent over about four years, while the most recent housing cycle peak in 1993/94 saw Sydney house prices rise by about 60 percent over two years. "I don't think we are going to see the sort of prices rises that we had in the 1980s and the 1993/94 period because we don't have the same sort of economic conditions that we had then," Crisp told Reuters. The Australian economy is currently going through a phase of low inflation and interest rates, which is not conducive to a housing boom, he said. "We don't have the same sort of economic conditions that we had in the 1980s and the 1993/94 period when we had high inflation and interest rates," Crisp said. The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has kept the official cash rate at a 14-year low of 6.0 percent since October 1996, after raising it 11 times in 1994 and 1995 to curb inflation. The RBA on Tuesday left the cash rate unchanged at 6.0 percent. Sydney and Melbourne house prices started to fall in late-1996 after the RBA started raising interest rates in late-1994. Sydney house prices fell by about 10 percent over the past year and Melbourne prices fell by about 7 percent, Crisp said. He said house prices in both cities were likely to start rising in the second half of 1997. "I think we are going to see house prices start to rise in the second half of this year and I think we are going to see some quite strong rises in 1998," Crisp said. He said housing market turnarounds were usually led by Sydney, which was Australia's largest market. Crisp said housing market conditions were likely to improve in Sydney with the economy continuing to grow strongly and interest rates likely to remain low. Melbourne's housing market was likely to follow Sydney's lead as the Victorian capital's economy improved, he said. Brisbane and Perth housing markets were likely to remain flat in 1997, he said. Sydney and Perth housing markets had both peaked in 1995, while the Brisbane market peaked in 1994, he said. Sydney house prices were likely to rise by about 15-20 percent over the next two years, Melbourne prices by about 10-15 percent and Brisbane and Perth prices to be flat, Crisp said. "I think we are going to see a more sedate housing market recovery over the next year or so." The housing market has been on the slide since the second half of 1995 as interest rates were raised to contain the highest inflation in nearly five years. The market was further hit by the end of the mining boom in Western Australia and the slowdown in the economy of the state of Queensland as large infrastructure projects were completed. The Sydney housing market was hit hardest with prices falling in some areas and the rate of increase slowing in others. But property experts said the market had bottomed out late last year and was now starting to recover as the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) cut interest rates to a nine-year low of 6.00 percent. "I think we have seen the worst of the Sydney housing market," said Michael Bannon, property analyst with the BNP Institute, a property research unit of BNP Paribas Australia. "I think we are going to see a gradual improvement in the Sydney market over the next 12 months." He said the same applied to the Perth housing market which had fallen the hardest of all the main Australian housing markets. "I think Perth is going to start to turn around in the second half of this year," Bannon said. He said the Brisbane and Melbourne housing markets were likely to continue to perform well. "I think we can expect a turnaround in the housing market in 1997 but it's not going to be the same as the 1980s boom or the 1993/94 peak," said Tim Lawless, senior economist with property analysts RP Data. "I don't think we can expect the same rate of price growth that we had in those two cycles." The housing market was in the doldrums in the early 1990s when the economy was in recession, but it staged a strong recovery in the 1993/94 cycle, with Sydney and Melbourne recording their biggest annual price rises since the 1980s boom. But the market turned down in late 1994, just as the RBA was starting to raise interest rates to curb inflation. "I don't think we are going to see prices soaring away again like we did in the 1980s or the 1993/94 cycle, but I do think we will see a reasonable improvement in housing market conditions," said Brian Bright, senior economist with the Commonwealth Bank of Australia. He said there were several reasons why the housing market was unlikely to repeat the past booms. "Firstly, we don't have the same level of economic growth that we had in the 1980s and the 1993/94 cycle," Bright said. "Secondly, we have got much higher interest rates than we had in the 1980s and the 1993/94 cycle, and thirdly, we have got much tighter credit conditions than we had in the 1980s and the 1993/94 cycle." The RBA raised the cash rate by a total of 200 basis points to 6.50 percent between August 1996 and January 1997, before leaving it on hold in the past two months. However, the RBA has signalled further rate rises are on the way to keep inflation within its target range of 2-4 percent. He said Brisbane and Perth were likely to record annual price rises of around 3-5 percent, while prices in Adelaide were likely to be flat. "I don't think we are going to see prices falling anywhere in Australia over the next 12 months," Lawless said. "I think we will see a reasonable improvement in the housing market, but I don't think we are going to see the same rate of price growth that we had in the 1980s or the 1993/94 cycle," Bright said.
