response: A potential new source of revenue -- oil -- offers hope of a fresh start for Chad's fragile economy as it rebuilds after three decades of war. President Idriss Deby, who heads Africa's largest nomadic nation with former French ties in the dry, sprawling area north-east of Cameroon, won a fifth term in office in polls ending in 1996. "Oil production will start in 2000," the president's British-based Petro-Lion consultant, David Forsyth, told Reuters. "We have 360 million barrels (15.3 billion tonnes) of proven reserves and 400 million barrels of probable reserves." Chad's 1993-97 stabilisation economic plan, backed by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, focuses on reviving agriculture, 80 percent of nomadic Chad's economy, and revitalising markets nomads pass through on their travels. "Agriculture is still the mainstay of Chad's economy but oil will be a welcome addition," World Bank economist for Chad, Jean-Claude thenon, told Report. "Oil revenues will be used to finance development and stabilise the budget." Chad's 1996/97 budget, based on 1995/96 commodity prices and 50 percent export revenues' contribution to the budget, is balanced but relies heavily on donor grants, thenon said. "Oil revenues will stabilise the budget and allow a gradual reduction of donor grants." Chad's 1993/97 plan targets inflation at 20 percent but 1996/97 inflation was 30 percent, thenon added. "Inflation will come down with a stable budget and the effects of harvest and market nomadic activity." Chad's 1993/97 plan aims for a 1996/97 credit growth of 20 percent but 1996/97 credit expansion was 40 percent, Bank of Chad governor, Jean-Bosco Tassadoh, said. "Credit expansion will come down with a stable budget and the effects of harvest and nomadic activity." Bank loans are mainly used for agriculture and trade business expansion. "Agriculture is expanding so credit will remain high but it will come down in 1997/98," Tassadoh added. "A balanced budget and the effects of nomadic activity will also help." Deby, a former guerrilla leader, French army officer and nomadic president pastoralist's paths interweave, won poll re-runs in 1996 after French-brokered runoff polls in March against former fellow guerral leader and former northern rival, Wadal Abdelkader Camo, now a southern rival's ally. French ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing monitored polls which French president Jacques Chirac's diplomats hoped would stabilise Chad's often volatile, sprawling, 80 nationality, 7.7 million-strong nation. 1997/98 focus is on budget, inflation and credit targets and an end to donor grants by 2000. "We are on track on all targets," thenon and Tassadoh said. Chad's 300-seat national assembly, 72 of whom had polls appointments, began work in 1997 after a 1997 legislative calendar's 45 nomadic constituency polls to fill former nomadic path gaps. Election polling units ranged from tree tents to town schools. "I am very happy to be back among my people," former northern constituency polls winner and former nomadic path rival, former northern army commander, Jean-Baptiste Mougoungui, told Reuters. "Oil will help us all." "God has given us oil so that we no longer depend on others," Deby told reporters in April, before a 15-nation summit on Chad's oil development plan. "Oil will above all allow us to become self-sufficient," he added. Chad, which borders Libya to the north, has 13,000-kilometre-long, often porous borders with 10 other African nations. It has long relied on volatile commodity prices, livestock and agriculture for income. "Oil will give Chad a new role in Africa and in the world," Deby said. French oil firm Total has a 30-year contract to explore and develop Chad's 12-block, 200,000 square-km (77,000 sq mi) northern sector, which accounts for 60 percent of pre-1990 French interest in African oil. British Petroleum has a 10-year contract for a 30 percent share of the 13th block to the south. French President Jacques Chirac, Dutch counterpart Wim Kok and other summit leaders welcomed Chad's progress towards stability and a return to full African and international obligations. "The time has come to rebuild Chad," Chirac told the summit. "We have all seen the problems Chad has had," Dutch leader Wim Kok told reporters. "But now it is getting more stable and we can do business with it," he added. Chad's pre-1990, French-backed export credits were worth 650 million dollars, including 350 million from France, then the world's biggest creditor. Chad had 3.3 billion dollars in international debt at the end of 1994, 27th of 39 African nations for total debt to exports ratio. "Oil will allow us to pay off our debt," Deby said. Chad's 1995/96 budget, based on 450 million dollars from agriculture, livestock, re-exports, commodity prices and donor grants, assumes oil revenue from 1996. Total's president in Chad, Jean-Marie Dauger, told Reuters last year that oil could flow to Port-Genton, Cameroon, by year end 1996, but no firm date was set. "Chad has 10 percent of African oil reserves so it will have a significant role in Africa," Dauger said. Chad's oil reserves are put at 1.5 billion barrels, 25th in the world. The 15-nation group, which includes oil consumers and producers, welcomed Chad's progress towards full international obligations but offered no loans or grants. "Chad is moving towards stability and we welcome that," German president and summit chairman Roman Herzog told reporters. "But we have no plans to give Chad any loans or grants." Chad has long-dry, southernmost border with oil producing neighbours Cameroon and Gabon. French exploration firms started looking for oil in Chad in the 1960s but left after finding little then. British firms had similar experiences in the 1930s. "There was nothing then but a long, dry, desert track to Cameroon," former Chad oil prospecting manager Jean-Pierre Ollivier told Reuters. "Everything has changed since then." French oil major Total, which has long Chadian contracts, is leading a consortium to develop Chad's 2,500-square-kilometre (1,000-square-mile) northern Permian block, which is estimated to have 250 million barrels of potential reserves. "Production could start by 2002," Total Chad manager Michel Mollien told Reuters. "That could earn Chad 150 million dollars a year in royalties and tax." Chad's 1997/98 provisional budget, which assumes 45 percent of revenue from oil, also assumes 270 million dollars in export earnings from cotton, 15 million from gum arabic, 20 million from livestock and 10 million from other produce. "Oil revenues will be put in a stabilisation account," Brouzet said. "Any use of revenues will depend on a borrowing policy yet to be defined by the president and finance ministry." Chad's banks had 1.5 billion francs (23 million dollars) in deposits at the end of 1997. "Any borrowing will have to be covered by exports," Brouzet added. "That will limit any borrowing to 23 million dollars." Chad's debt stood at 350 million dollars at the end of 1997. "Any new borrowing will have to be agreed by lenders under a London club debt reduction plan," he added. "That will limit any borrowing to 23 million dollars." Chad's former rivals, including Wadal Abdelkader Kamougou, all congratulated Deby after poll end. Deby, a former army sergeant, former northern guerrid leader and long-time French ally, will fly French former rival president Jacques Chirac on Sunday for a 50th anniversary of French independence in Algeria. "Oil will be a real plus from 1999," Brouzet repeated. "Agricultural produce will continue to be important but will not account for 90 percent of revenues as once planned." Chad's southernmost 1,100-kilometre (680-mile) border with oil producing neighbours Cameroon and Gabon is 120 kilometres (75 miles) at its nearest. response: Ivory Coast has received three formal proposals for building new cocoa processing factories but no approvals have yet been notified, Ivorian Commodities Minister Guy Alain-Gauze said on Friday. "Proposals are not approvals," he told Reuters in a telephone interview. "We are studying them." Dutch firm Mariko/Koninklijke Algemene Cocoa Industrie (KACI), Swiss group Petra Cargo, and a third, Ivorian-British venture called Ivory Cocoa have put forward plans, Gauze said. "Two of the proposals concern San Pedro and one Abidjan." Ivory Coast's light cocoa export season runs from mid-August to mid-March. San Pedro is a cocoa port 65 km (40 miles) west of Ivory Coast's largest city, Abidjan. "San Pedro has a real need for a local processor because of the volume of beans," Gauze said. "San Pedro's cocoa exporters are often forced to put up with 70 or 80 percent humidity levels before beans are shipped because local storage capacities are not sufficient." Ivory Cocoa's proposal for a 20,000-tonne factory at Abidjan's port is the third and latest to reach Ivory Coast's commodities and industrial promotion bodies, Gauze said. "The other two proposals are for 50,000 tonnes each for San Pedro." Ivory Cocoa's proposal is the most advanced as it has already signed local agreements, Gauze said. "They have an 18-million dollar loan agreement with the British Export-Import Bank." Ivory Cocoa's managing director, British national John Hall, told Reuters in Abidjan on Friday that he hoped to start construction in January and have the plant up and running by mid-1997. Dutch firm Mariko, which already has a 30,000-tonne plant in San Pedro, plans to expand this and add a further 20,000 tonnes in new plant nearby, Gauze said. "Mariko's proposals are off local balance accounts of Ivory Coast's CACI bank." Swiss firm Petra, which has 25,000 tonnes of cocoa storage capacity at San Pedro, plans a 50,000-tonne plant nearby, Gauze said. Petra's proposal is off local accounts of Ivory Coast's BICO bank, he added. Gauze said promotions committee members would meet Ivory Cocoa on Monday, Mariko on Tuesday and Petra on Wednesday to study the proposals in detail. "We will then make our recommendations to our approval bodies." Ivory Cocoa's Hall told Reuters in Abidjan that he was confident of approval. "Ivory Cocoa's proposal is the most advanced because it is the most concrete," he said. I believe that the Catholic Church does need to change its ways in order to remain a vital part of life in the 21st century.  The first and most obvious way this needs to be done is through the ordination of married men and women to the priesthood in certain circumstances. The current policy, known as the “Latin Rite,” only allows unmarried men to become priests in the Western (Latin Rite) branch of the Church. Other rites, such as the Eastern Orthodox and the Eastern Rite Catholic Churches, do allow for married men to become priests in their respective branches. The argument for this can be made on several grounds. First, it would allow for the ordination of men who have fathered children while living in various forms of sin prior to marriage. This would not only bring those men into the Church in a legitimate way, but also bring their families (often large ones) into the Church as well. Second, it would allow for the ordination of men who have served as deacons in the Latin Rite while married, and who have since been widowed or divorced.  Another way the Church needs to change is through the loosening of its strict rules regarding birth control and the ordination of women. The current policy, known as the “Pauline” or “Latin Rite” policy, forbids the use of any form of birth control other than the “rhythm method.” This is an outdated and frequently ineffective means of preventing pregnancy. Allowing married couples to use other forms of birth control would not only help to prevent unwanted pregnancies, but also help to prevent abortions in cases where a pregnancy would be a hardship for the family (financially, emotionally, etc.).  Allowing the ordination of women would not only help to prevent the situations I described in the previous paragraph, but would also bring a whole new perspective to the Church. Women make up about half of the total number of Christians in the world, and only a very small percentage of those are Catholic. Allowing women to become priests would help to bring more of that half into the Church, and would also help to change the perspective of the Church as a whole. The current male-dominated hierarchy of the Church has a very skewed perspective on the needs and desires of the female half of the Christian population.  Finally, the Church needs to change in the way it views and interacts with other Christian denominations. The current attitude, known as “extra-calced” or “non-infallible” ecumenism, has been in place since the Second Vatican Council. This means that while the Church is open to dialogue and interaction with other denominations, it still holds itself to be the one true Church and the others to be various forms of error. A more open-minded attitude, one which would view other denominations as various forms of the same Truth, would be much healthier and more productive for all involved.  In conclusion, I believe that the Catholic Church does need to change its ways in order to remain a vital part of life in the 21st century. The changes I have outlined here, while radical to some, are not only necessary, but would also be beneficial to the Church as a whole. The Church, like any other institution, must be open to change in order to remain relevant.

response: The long-awaited turnaround in Australia's housing market is expected to occur during 1997 but it is unlikely to signal a repeat of the boom seen in the 1980s or the most recent peak in the 1993/94 year, analysts and economists said on Monday. "I think we're going to see a housing market recovery in 1997, but it's not going to be a boom because we don't have the ingredients for a boom," said Tim Moore, senior economist with BNP Paribas. "We don't have the low interest rates that we had in the 1980s and we don't have the strong economic growth that we had in the 1980s." Moore said housing market conditions had improved with interest rates falling to 10-year lows and a stabilisation of the housing market in Sydney, Australia's largest market. "I think Sydney is probably through the worst of its cycle, I think it has probably seen the bottom in housing market terms," Moore said. "I don't think we are going to see any further falls in Sydney housing prices and I think we are going to see some modest rises over the course of 1997." Moore said the housing market in Melbourne, Australia's second largest market, had also bottomed out and was expected to start rising in 1997. "I think the other major markets, Brisbane and Perth, I think they are going to continue to underperform the Sydney and Melbourne markets," Moore said. "I don't think we are going to see any significant rises in Brisbane and Perth housing markets over the course of 1997." The housing market in Brisbane had been over-supplied for some time and the same situation was now developing in Perth, Moore said. "I don't think we are going to see any significant rises in housing market terms in either Brisbane or Perth until we see some improvement in the economic conditions in those cities," Moore said. Economist Peter Burnet at the Australia Institute said there was no prospect of a housing market boom like the one seen in the 1980s when housing prices rose dramatically in Sydney and Melbourne. "I don't think we are going to see anything like that again because we don't have the same sort of conditions that we had back then," Burnet said. "We don't have the same sort of economic conditions, we don't have the same sort of interest rate conditions and we don't have the same sort of policy conditions." Burnet said there was no prospect of a repeat of the most recent housing market peak in 1993/94 when housing markets in Sydney and Melbourne started to turn down in late 1993. "We are not going to see anything like that again because we don't have the same sort of conditions that we had back then," Burnet said. "We have had a period of fairly steady housing market conditions over the last couple of years and I think we are going to see a continuation of that over the next year or so." The housing market turnaround was expected to provide a boost to the Australian economy, economists said. "I think the housing market recovery is going to add to economic growth in 1997, it is not going to be the main driver of economic growth but it is going to add to economic growth," Moore said. "I think we are going to see a pick-up in housing market related industries and I think we are going to see a pick-up in consumer spending as people feel more confident about the housing market." The Australian housing market had been in the doldrums over the past couple of years with prices falling in Sydney and Melbourne and little or no growth in other markets. The housing market has been a concern for the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) which has cut interest rates to 10-year lows to try to stimulate the market. The RBA on Monday left its official interest rate unchanged at 6.50 percent, a level it has held since October 1996. The local housing market has also been affected by uncertainty over the future direction of the Australian economy, with the economy expected to grow at its slowest rate in 16 years in 1996. However, economists are forecasting a pick-up in economic growth in 1997. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800 61-2 9373-1900 fax 61-2 9373-1918 ------------------------------------------------------------------- The Australian -- Home Page ----------------------------------------------------------------

input: Write an approximately 500 word essay to the following prompt: Do you feel that gender discrimination is still an issue in the present-day United States?
target_task: Write an approximately 500 word essay to the following prompt: Do you feel that gender discrimination is still an issue in the present-day United States?

response:
I do feel that gender discrimination is still an issue in the present-day United States but I believe that the definition of gender discrimination has changed. Back in the day gender discrimination was straight forward, women couldn't have jobs men didn't want, women only worked as secretaries if they chose a career. Nowadays women can be a president of the United States but that doesn't mean that the small details of gender discrimination have disappeared. I believe that women are discriminated against in the area of having a family if they choose a career in a corporation. I saw this discrimination first hand in my internship this past summer. I worked alongside men who had children and they never once spoke about their children while they worked, but I as a woman who has no children yet felt pressured to work about my hypothetical children. My supervisor would ask me questions like if I had a sister who looked like me that I could use as a model for an upcoming shoot, and then she would add on if this hypothetical sister didn't want to model would I? I felt trapped and discriminated against because I felt like I couldn't say no because of my possible future role as a mother. Also I felt like I couldn't say yes because I didn't want to give up my career. I don't want to have to choose between having a family and having a career. But according to society and my supervisor I do have to choose because they don't believe that I can have both. I watched this same discrimination happen to my mother, she was a nurse in the army and had to give up her career once she had me because the army doesn't allow children in the army. Now I want to join the military with my husband and we want to have children, and I feel like I'm stuck in the middle of this no-mans-land of having a family and a career. But I do believe that there are institutions like the Women's Studies Center that are trying to prevent discrimination like the kind I experienced. The WSC offers programs like “Women in the Military” where they try and figure out ways for women to have a career in the military and have children, which is exactly what I want. So even though I feel discriminated against I still have hope that there are places like the WSC that believe that women should have the right to choose a career and have a family. 

Furthermore, there are other areas of gender discrimination that are still present in our society. For example, are movies and TV shows. In the media women are still portrayed as the submissive sex, the one that needs to be saved, and the one that is sexually promiscuous. In the 2006 movie Firehouse Dog, for example, there is a clear gender discrimination. In the movie the main character, a man, is a heroic firefighter, but the woman firefighters in the movie are portrayed as sexual objects and are only concerned with their looks. This is a clear example of how women in the media are still discriminated against. Women are either made to look like we are weak and need a man to save us or we are made to look like we are sexually promiscuous. 

In conclusion, I do believe that gender discrimination is still present in our society but I believe that the definition of gender discrimination has changed. Women now aren't discriminated against because of their gender but instead are discriminated against because of the role that society has created for women. Women are discriminated against if they want to have a career and a family because society believes that women can't handle both. And in the media women are discriminated against because they are either made to look weak or sexually promiscuous. But like I said before there are institutions like the Women's Studies Center that are trying to prevent discrimination like the kind I experienced and discrimination like what is seen in the media. So while we may not live in a society where women can't be a president but we do live in a society where women have to choose between having a career and having a family if they choose a career in a corporation. But I remain hopeful that one day I will be able to have both a family and a career without being discriminated against.

"The fuel surcharge was not universally accepted on all trade lanes and at all cargo prices so it was quite chaotic trying to keep it. I think the airlines have decided to try and stabilise cargo prices through a period of rate increases instead. It will be interesting to see if the attempt at a new round of ad hoc cargo rate increases is successful this time around. I would expect it to be more disciplined and with a better chance of being sustained if it is confined to Europe/Middle East then Atlantic trade. The recent round of fuel surcharge attempts was more global and I believe that trying to impose it on a truly global trade such as Asia Pacific to Europe/Middle East was a major factor in it not being successful. I also believe that the current attempt at a new round of ad hoc rate increases will be more focused on the ex Europe/Middle East prime belly trade where I believe there is a reasonable chance of it being successful. response: Cathay Pacific Airways Limited is the first airline to test fly a new'sharks skin' aircraft coating which could reduce fuel costs and revolutionise air travel, a Cathay spokeswoman told Reuters. The Hong Kong Koolspeake Slot 46 round the clock service through a 10 Hong Kong Coin ad hoc trial is using a specially modified Boing 747-405 flight with the new coating from New Zealand's Air New Zealand trial period is expected to last for two to three months. The sharkskin or more precisely the New Zealand developed 'Raupeku' coating is made from a natural mineral composite material which is applied to the aircraft's fusage and wings in a wave like pattern. The manufacturers say it replicates the surface texture of a shark's skin which is believed to reduce aerodynamic drag and thus save fuel. The New Zealand consortium which developed the coating is called 'Made in New Zealand' and is made up of Air New Zealand, the state owned Industrial Research Ltd and the Massey University. The consortium says the coating is not a paint and is not a film. It is a permanent part of the aircraft's surface and is not affected by temperature changes. The Raupeku coating is also claimed to be twice as effective as the current best aircraft coating. If the trial is successful, Cathay is expected to buy a 21 percent share in the New Zealand consortium for US108 million. A statement from the consortium said a deal on a share sale was'subject to contract' and 'no agreement had yet been reached'. target_task: What are some benefits of learning a new language?

response:
Learning a new language opens up many opportunities for personal and professional growth. Some benefits include:

1. Improved cognitive abilities: Studies show that bilingual individuals have better focus and multitasking skills. Learning a new language also helps improve memory and problem-solving abilities.

9. Increased creativity: Studies suggest that bilingual individuals are more creative than monolingual individuals. Learning a new language can help expand your thinking and problem-solving abilities.

10. Opportunity to meet new people: Learning a new language can help you connect with new people from different backgrounds. It can broaden your social circle and help you make new friends.

There are several ways to reduce food waste at home. Here are some tips:

1. Plan your meals: Make a weekly meal plan based on what you have in your pantry, fridge, and freezer. This will help you use the ingredients before they go bad.

2. Shop smart: Make a list before you go shopping and stick to it. Buy only what you need and use frequently.

3. Store food properly: Make sure you're storing your food correctly to maximize its shelf life. For example, some fruits and vegetables should be stored in the fridge, while others should be kept at room temperature.

4. Use leftovers: Get creative with your leftovers. Turn them into new meals or freeze them for later.

5. Donate or share: If you have food that you won't be able to use before it goes bad, consider donating it to a local food bank or sharing it with neighbors or coworkers.

6. Compost: If you have a garden, consider composting your food scraps instead of throwing them away. This will help reduce the amount of waste you produce and provide nutrients for your garden.

7. Buy imperfect produce: Instead of throwing away perfectly good produce because it's not perfect, buy imperfect produce. Many grocery stores offer discounts on imperfect produce, and it's just as nutritious as the perfect stuff.

8. Preserve food: Preserve food by canning, freezing, or dehydrating it. This will help you use seasonal produce all year round and reduce the amount of food you throw away.

There are several common misconceptions about climate change. Here are some of them:

1. Climate change is a hoax: This is one of the most pervasive misconceptions. Some people believe that climate change is not real or that it's a hoax perpetuated by governments or scientists. However, there is a large body of scientific evidence that shows climate change is real and that human activities are contributing to it.

2. Human activities don't contribute to climate change: Some people believe that natural factors, such as volcanic eruptions, are the primary cause of climate change. While it's true that natural factors can influence the climate, the overwhelming evidence shows that human activities, such as burning fossil fuels, are the main drivers of current climate change.

3. Climate change isn't happening right now: Some people believe that climate change is a problem that will happen in the future, but it's not something we need to worry about right now. However, climate change is already happening and it's having real-world impacts. For example, we're seeing more frequent and intense weather events, melting glaciers, and rising sea levels.

4. It's too late to do anything about climate change: Some people believe that it's too late to take action to address climate change. However, there are still things we can do to reduce our carbon footprint and mitigate the worst impacts of climate change. For example, we can transition to renewable energy sources, improve energy efficiency, and reduce our use of single-use plastics.

5. Climate change isn't a big deal: Some people believe that climate change isn't a big deal or that it's not worth worrying about. However, the impacts of climate change could be catastrophic. For example, rising sea levels could displace millions of people, and extreme weather events could cause billions of dollars in damage. It's important that we take action to address climate change now, before it's too late.

There are several ways to reduce food waste at home. Here are some tips:

1. Plan your meals: Make a weekly meal plan and shop accordingly. This will help you buy only what you need and use everything you buy.

2. Store food properly: Make sure you are storing your food correctly. Different foods need different storage conditions to stay fresh. For example, fruits and vegetables should be kept in the refrigerator, while grains and pasta should be stored in a cool, dry place.

3. Use your freezer: Freeze extra portions of cooked food or fresh produce that you won't be able to use before it goes bad. This is a great way to preserve food and reduce waste.

4. Use your leftovers: Make it a habit to use your leftovers instead of letting them go to waste. Get creative with your meals and find new ways to use up your extra food.

5. Compost: If you have a garden, consider starting a compost pile. This is a great way to reduce food waste by turning kitchen scraps into nutrient-rich soil for your garden.

6. Donate: If you have extra food that you won't be able to use before it goes bad, consider donating it to a local food bank or soup kitchen. This is a great way to help those in need and reduce food waste at the same time. 

7. Shop smart: When you go shopping, try to buy only what you need and avoid buying in bulk unless you know you will use it all. Also, try to buy produce that is in season and locally grown to reduce transportation emissions and ensure freshness. 

8. Use every part: Try to use every part of the food you buy. For example, vegetable scraps can be used to make stock, and stale bread can be used to make breadcrumbs. 

9. Plan for imperfect produce: Try to buy produce that is slightly imperfect or misshapen. This produce is often discounted and still perfectly edible, but it won't look as pretty on the shelf. 

10. Be mindful: Try to be more mindful of the food you buy and the food you have at home. Make a conscious effort to use up what you have before buying more, and try to avoid overbuying or impulse purchases.

response:

2. Use what you have: Before going grocery shopping, check what you already have in your pantry, fridge, and freezer and plan meals around those ingredients.

3. Store food properly: Make sure you are storing your food correctly to prolong its freshness. Different foods need different storage conditions.

4. Use your freezer: Freeze foods before they go bad. You can freeze fruits and vegetables, cook extra rice or pasta, and even freeze leftovers.

"They (Chinese buyers) have gone completely," a Hong Kong-based trader said. "The market has gone too far, too fast." Shanghai soymeal hit a record high of US$325/tonne on Tuesday, up US$10 from the previous day's close, on tight supplies and strong demand from China. China's soybean crushing industry, which accounts for more than 60 percent of the world's total volume, has been a major buyer of soymeal in recent months, as it grinds its own beans to meet export orders. But traders said the industry had not made any significant purchases in recent days because of the high prices. "They are not buying anything now," a Beijing trader said. "They have enough stock in hand. They have been waiting for the price to come back." The Chinese market has been volatile in recent weeks on tight supplies and heavy export orders. Traders said a cargo of 80,000 tonnes of Brazilian soybeans, which arrived in Tianjin last week, had been sold as high-priced soymeal. China's customs bureau confirmed the shipment, but would not say who had ordered it. Traders said the beans had been bought by a state-owned trading company for shipment to Indonesia. But Indonesian buyers were reported to have baulked at the high price, and the beans were now being offered to other Asian markets. Customs said in a faxed statement that the Chinese market was "quite tight" because of heavy export orders, which had been placed before the recent price rises. The United States said last week 130,000 tonnes of soybeans had been sold to China, with another 100,000 tonnes in the pipeline. Traders said this shipment was now being held up by Chinese customs, which was demanding a phytosanitary certificate. Customs would not confirm this. response: China is awash with steel and suppliers scrambling for a piece of one of the world's few active markets kept prices down, traders and industry executives in Asia said on Tuesday. "China is in a panic to get rid of steel," a trader in Singapore with a Chinese steel mill source said. "Prices are under pressure because of the huge volume of material coming out of China," he said. China's steel exports surged in July, the first full month after the government lifted a ban on shipments intended to help state-owned mills pay for raw material. The ban was in place to prevent environmental damage caused by the industry's high energy consumption and heavy polluting, but industry sources said it was also aimed at reducing excess capacity. China's steel industry, the world's largest, has been plagued by overcapacity for years, exacerbated by a drive to meet export targets and ramp up industrial production. "The export ban was a good thing for the industry, but it was only in place for a few months," a Shanghai-based industry source said. "The problem is the industry can't be run on a month-by-month basis," he said. China's steel export tonnage in July was up 35 percent on June, customs data showed, with destinations including the United States, Indonesia, South Korea and Taiwan. "The material going to the Americas is very low-grade," a trader in Hong Kong said. "China is desperate to get rid of it," he said. "The Americas is the only market at the moment," he said. Other traders said the material going to the United States was in the form of scrap, a traditional export market for China. But a source at a major Chinese scrap processor said shipments to the United States had been put on hold while the industry waited for the outcome of a probe by the US Environmental Protection Agency into illegal exports of Chinese steel scrap. "The scrap industry is on a very nervous footing right now," he said. "The EPA has been very secretive about what they are doing," he said. "The industry is waiting for some kind of clarification before they start shipping again," he said. Other traders said China's steel exports to Europe had been affected by a 15 percent duty imposed on hot-rolled coil in June. The duty was imposed to protect the industry from massive dumping by Russia, traders said. "The Chinese material is cheap and the Europeans have no other source of material at the moment," a trader in Europe said. "But they are not going to buy more than they need because of the duty," he said. response: China is awash with steel and suppliers scrambling for a piece of one of the world's few active markets kept prices down, traders and industry executives in Asia said on Tuesday. "China is exporting on a very large scale, and I think they are trying to get rid of their inventories," a trader in Hong Kong said. "The Chinese have huge stocks and they want to get rid of them before the end of the year," a source in Singapore said. China's steel exports rose in October to 2.3 million tonnes, up from 1.9 million tonnes in September, customs statistics showed. The increase came after Beijing in August banned steel exports in an attempt to preserve domestic stocks and prop up prices. The ban was not enforced, however, and traders said it was instigated by the State Planning Commission to cover a large and unexpected increase in steel production. "The Chinese are now going back to their old ways, and they are not concerned about the environmental issue," a trader in Hong Kong said. "They are producing and exporting to make money. "The Chinese government is not in control," he said. The Asian market is in need of around 1.5 million tonnes of steel in the last two months of the year, traders said. This is because of orders from Japan, which is rebuilding after September's earthquake and tsunami, and South Korea, which is gearing up for the new-year shipbuilding season. "There is a lot of demand from Japan and Korea, but the problem is the money," a trader in Singapore said. "The Japanese and Korean buyers are waiting for the insurance money. "They have placed orders, but they have not paid," he said. "The Chinese are not prepared to wait, so they are looking for other buyers." Traders said the Chinese were offering steel on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, meaning they would pay the freight and loading costs. This is a departure from the usual practice of the buyer paying, and is aimed at attracting business, traders said. "The Chinese are desperate to sell," a trader in Hong Kong said. "They are offering FOB, which is unheard of. "They are trying to get rid of their stocks, and they don't care if they make a loss," he said. Traders said Chinese steel exports in November and December could reach 3 million tonnes, but this would depend on who the Chinese could find to buy. "The problem is, who is going to take it?" a trader in Singapore said. "The Chinese steel is not wanted in Europe or the United States because of anti-dumping duties. "The Southeast Asian markets are small and cannot take that much," he said. "The Chinese have to look to the far-east markets, but these markets cannot take 3 million tonnes," he said. "The Chinese have to find someone, because they have to get rid of their stocks before the end of the year. "The Chinese steel industry is in a mess," he said. "They have no control. "They have no idea what they are doing," he said. "China is still pushing its steel exports and will not stop until it exhausts its stocks," a trader in Singapore with a Chinese steel mill source said. "Prices are under pressure because of China," a trader in Hong Kong said. China's steel exports in the first two months of the year came in at 3.4 million tonnes, up from 2.6 million tonnes in December, customs statistics showed. Traders said a lot of that steel was going to Southeast Asia. "The Chinese are desperate to get rid of their steel," a trader in Taiwan said. "They are offering very low prices, under $US200 a tonne for hot-rolled coil," he said. That was less than the cost of production in China, traders said. "But the Chinese have so much steel they don't know what to do with," a trader in Hong Kong said. "They are not concerned about prices. They just want to get rid of the metal," he said. China's steel industry has been plagued with overcapacity, estimated by some industry sources at as much as 50 million tonnes a year. The government has announced a series of measures to cut that excess, including the closure of 100 small and inefficient mills in the first quarter. But that process has not yet begun, traders said. "The Chinese are not going to stop exporting until they run out of stocks," the trader in Singapore said. "They are not concerned about the environmental inspections. They will just find a way around them," he said. The Chinese embassy in Canberra confirmed reports from Southeast Asia that China was issuing export permits for up to one million tonnes of steel a month. "China is a big country and has a big population and a big industry, and it needs raw materials and components to keep production going," a Chinese embassy official in Canberra said. "So of course it is going to export," he said. But he said the idea that China was dumping steel on the world market at any price was wrong. "China is not going to sell its steel for less than cost," he said. "The Chinese industry is a business, it is not a charity," he said. He said the current global economic downturn was a problem for all steel exporters, not just China. "The whole world steel industry is in trouble," he said. "The European Union is in recession, Japan is in recession, the United States is in recession. Who is going to buy their steel?" he said. "The world needs to find a way to deal with this problem, and that is not by pointing the finger at China," he said. But traders in Asia said the current global economic malaise was not the only factor keeping steel prices down. "The world steel markets are being kept in balance by China," a trader in Hong Kong said. "Without China, the whole world steel industry would go bust," he said. "But with China, the industry can keep going," he said. "China is the saviour of the steel industry," he said. "Without China, who would buy the scrap metal?" he said. Traders in Asia said they expected Chinese steel exports to continue, perhaps even pick up, in the current quarter. "The Chinese have a lot of steel they need to get rid of," a trader in Taiwan said. "They are not going to stop," he said. "They have got used to exporting now," he said. "They are not going to go back on that," he said. "The Chinese are a very stubborn people," he said. "They will not be told what to do," he said. "And they have so much steel they don't know what to do with," he said. "So they will keep on exporting," he said. "And if the rest of the world does not want their steel, well, that is not China's problem," he said. response: China is awash with steel and suppliers scrambling for a piece of one of the world's few active markets kept prices down, traders and industry executives in Asia said on Tuesday. Chinese mills have been pushing exports to the United States and Europe in the face of slack domestic demand, a source in Hong Kong with a major steel trader said. "The Chinese are really trying to push tonnes on us," he said, adding that a recent cargo of 20,000 tonnes of hot-rolled coil had been offered to his company at a price of $US240 a tonne. That was $US20 below the price of the previous cargo, he said. Other traders said prices being asked by the Chinese ranged from $US230 to $US250 a tonne for hot-rolled coil, and $US210 to $US230 a tonne for cold-rolled coil. "They are desperate to sell," a trader in Singapore said. "They have got all this steel on their hands and they have got to get it out," he said. Chinese mills have been ramping up production in recent months, encouraged by Beijing's call for industrial expansion and increased exports. The country's steel industry has been in expansion mode since the second half of last year, and has been producing at a rate of 40 million tonnes a year. But demand has failed to keep pace, and the industry is now facing a mountain of excess steel, industry sources said. A major Chinese steel executive said recently that the industry was facing a loss of $US1 billion in the first quarter of this year. The Chinese embassy in Brussels said in a statement in late March that China's steel exports to the European Union in the first two months of the year were up 42.6 percent on the same period in 1998 to 1.8 million tonnes. The embassy said China's steel exports to the United States in the first two months of this year were up 61.4 percent on the same period in 1998 to 800,000 tonnes. Traders said the Chinese were now targeting the United States, which has high-level talks on China's accession to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) scheduled for late April. The United States is the biggest market for steel, and took 15.3 million tonnes of imports in 1998, according to the International Steel Institute. But the US market is dominated by the three big integrated producers -- Bethlehem Steel Corp, United States Steel Corp and Nucor Corp -- and they have been vocal in their opposition to cheap imports. The United States has slapped anti-dumping and countervailing duties on a range of steel products from China, and the two sides have been embroiled in a bitter tit-for-tat trade dispute. The Chinese have been offering steep discounts to get their steel into the American market, traders said. But the US integrated producers have been able to hold out, and the Chinese cargos have been sitting in warehouses in the United States, traders said. The Chinese embassy in Brussels said China's steel exports to the European Union in the first two months of this year were down 12.5 percent on the same period in 1998. The European Union took 17.5 million tonnes of steel imports in 1998, according to the International Steel Institute. The Chinese have been offering steep discounts on their steel to get it into the European Union market, traders said. But the European Union has been in the process of setting up a common external tariff on steel, which will come into effect on July 1. The common tariff will be set at a level to keep out cheap, surplus steel exports from countries like China, traders said. The Chinese embassy in Brussels said the common external tariff would be "a protectionist measure" and would harm the relationship between China and the European Union. The Chinese steel industry is hoping for a pick-up in domestic demand, and has been pinning its hopes on the government's $US320 billion infrastructure spending programme. But that has yet to materialise, and the industry is facing a massive oversupply problem, industry sources said. The Chinese mills are now looking to the few active markets in the world to get rid of their excess steel, traders and industry executives said. The pick-up in exports to the United States and Europe will help, they said. "They are desperate for business," a trader in Hong Kong said. "They have got a huge amount of steel on their hands and they have got to get it out." (US$1 = 8.3 yuan)

"There's been some talk of 10,000 tonnes, but I don't know," a trader in Hong Kong said. "But it's not going to be 50,000 tonnes. I think that's a little bit of Hong Kong gossip." Chinese importers had been booking small cargoes of soyoil in recent weeks, traders said, but it was not clear if this was because of growing demand or a lack of availability of other products such as meal. "The Chinese are booking small parcels of everything at the moment," a trader in Southeast Asia said. "But it's very hard to get a straight answer out of them." Traders said soyoil orders had been cancelled because the shipments were expected to arrive before the current lot of bookings, and the Chinese had already run out of storage space. But this was not likely to be a trend-setting event, they said. "The Chinese have a lot of cargo on the books at the moment," a trader in Singapore said. response: Canada's Barrick Gold Corp. appeared to regain the upper hand on Tuesday in the perplexing fight for control of the massive Busang gold find in Indonesia. The Toronto-based company said it had reached an understanding with the Indonesian government to form a new venture, called Barrick (Busang) Ltd, to operate Busang. Under the arrangement, Barrick would keep 75 percent of Busang and invest US$125 million in the new company. The government would get 25 percent. "This is a very positive development," Barrick chairman Peter Munk said in a telephone interview. "We've been given an opportunity to move forward with this great property." But it was not clear if the Indonesian government would accept the arrangement without the involvement of a controversial figure who has claimed control of Busang. Suwarno, also known as Tuti, said he was "disappointed" by Barrick's latest move. "I will not give up my struggle to regain my rights," he said in a statement issued through his lawyer in Toronto. But Barrick and the Indonesian government say Suwarnas claims are baseless. The fight over Busang has left Barrick with its reputation battered and its stock price depressed. The company has spent more than US$300 million exploring and developing Busang, located in the eastern part of Indonesia's South Sulawesi province. Experts say the find has at least 20 million ounces of gold and possibly as much as 40 million. To keep the Indonesian government happy, Barrick also said it would give the government 10 percent of the gold produced from Busang. response: The glory of controlling Busang, one of the world's richest gold deposits, has thrown together an unlikely duo. Toronto-based Bre-X Minerals Ltd. and Calgary-based Barrick Gold Corp. were forged into partners last week when Bre-X, the discoverer of Busang in Indonesia, was left struggling under the weight of its discovery. "Bre-X has got itself into a bit of a bind," said gold analyst Peter Grosskopf of Toronto's Research Capital Corp. "They needed help and they got it." Under the terms of their deal, Barrick will operate Busang and the two companies will share the gold discovery 50-50. Bre-X will receive C$175 million ($136 million) in cash and 12 million Barrick shares worth C$136 million. Bre-X also got the right to buy one million Barrick shares over the next three years at C$136 each. "This is a very fair deal for Bre-X shareholders," said Bre-X chairman Ed Dayo. "It gives us the opportunity to unlock the value of Busang without taking on any more debt." But Bre-X investors were not so sure. The company's stock dropped C$1.40 to C$7.25 in heavy trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange Monday. "The market is interpreting this as a takeover and Bre-X did not get a premium," said gold analyst John Ing of Maison Placements Inc. "They got their operating cash cost and that's it." Ing said Barrick has an operating cost for Busang of about C$200 an ounce. The latest estimate for the deposit is 33.7 million ounces of gold so far. Ing said the cost to Barrick to bring the gold out of the ground is about C$335 an ounce. The market is assuming the number will go up, he said. "The market is being very cautious." But Ing said he is very bullish on Busang. He has a personal estimate of 50 million ounces of gold. "I'm very happy with the deal," he said. Barrick also has an arrangement with Newmont Mining Corp. to explore for gold on Busang. If Barrick finds more than 25 million ounces of gold, Bre-X will get 1 percent of the total production. If the total is between 25 million and 35 million ounces, Bre-X gets 0.5 percent. "This is a very good arrangement for Bre-X," Ing said. But gold analyst Grosskopf said he is more cautious. He has a personal estimate of 35 million ounces of gold on Busang. "I think the upside is capped," he said. response: The glory of controlling Busang, one of the world's richest gold deposits, has thrown together an unlikely duo. In one corner is Peter Munk, the suave but aggressive founder of heavyweight Barrick Gold Corp., backed by buckets of money, power, connections and experience. In the other is David Walsh, the maverick chief of Bre-X Minerals Ltd., the young Canadian exploration firm that discovered Busang in the jungles of East Kalimantan on the Indonesian island of Borneo. The Indonesian government has told Barrick and Bre-X to form a joint venture to manage the fabulous gold find. But the government edict would force an unnatural David-and-Goliath alliance on two companies led by two very different men. To observers, Munk, 69, is the epitome of class. He makes sure everything is top-notch and pays top dollar. Barrick's imposing office towers over downtown Toronto, impressing visitors with its grandiosity. Those who know him best say Munk plays to win. In sports, he sticks to skiing and tennis, believing that focusing on just two activities will help him excel. With Barrick, North America's biggest gold company and Munk's baby, he sticks doggedly to gold, refusing to diversify into other metals or minerals. "He's like a tiger," his long-time friend Bob Smith, the recently retired president of Barrick, told Reuters. "If he grabs hold of something, he won't let go. He has a tremendous ability to focus, whether it's recreation or business." In the 1950s, Munk, originally from Hungary, started up Clairtone Sound Corp., a stereo company that dazzled Canada until it flopped in 1971. "Everything I've done afterward has been child's play compared with Clairtone," he told author Peter Newman. "What I learned was never to give away your destiny." In 1983, Munk started Barrick, producing 3,000 ounces a year, and built it into the world's third largest gold company with estimated production of 3.2 million ounces for 1996. Bre-X's Walsh has gone from rags to riches in less than four years. He started as a Montreal stockbroker, was transferred to Calgary, Alberta in the 1980s and then broke out on his own. He concentrated on oil and gas exploration and then switched to mining. But by 1993, his exploration efforts had dried up. "We had these claims which were worthless, and no money," Walsh, 51, told Reuters in a recent interview. Almost broke, he scraped together C$10,000 ($7,400) to start exploring in Indonesia, pursuading friends to invest C$200,000 ($148,000) for a stake in the area now known as the central Busang. Walsh hit the jackpot with Busang, which has at least 57 million ounces of gold, currently worth $20 billion. "It just kept growing," Walsh said. "By July and August (1995) it really appeared it would be a monster discovery." He ran Bre-X from the basement of his Calgary home until last year. Bre-X's rocketing stock has made him a multi-millionaire and he now lives in the Bahamas with his wife Jeannette. But he has one regret. "We should have been more visible in Indonesia," he said. "I think where we lacked was in making more relationships than we had in Indonesia." Bre-X has an alliance with Sigit Harjojudan, the son of Indonesian President Suharto, but observers said Sigit's influence was eclipsed by that of his sister Siti Hardiyanti, with whom Barrick forged an early alliance. Munk has attracted to his advisory board former U.S. President George Bush, former Canadian Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and former Bundesbank President Karl Otto Poehl. He has ties with politicians in many countries and analysts said those gave him the upper hand with Busang. Munk and Walsh have tried to tango before. In 1994, they reached an agreement on developing Busang. But last-minute changes from Barrick prompted Bre-X to back out of the deal. With Barrick's rival Placer Dome Inc. trying to woo the Indonesian government into allowing it to bid on Bre-X, Walsh has made it clear he would rather do business with Placer than with Barrick.

response: Canada's Barrick Gold Corp. appeared to regain the upper hand on Tuesday in the perplexing fight for control of the massive Busang gold find in Indonesia. The company said the Indonesian mining ministry had approved its plan to operate Busang, including its arrangement with Australia's Bre-X Minerals Ltd to fund development in exchange for a stake in the discovery. "This is a significant step forward," Barrick chairman Peter Munk said in a telephone interview. "I think we're on our way." But Barrick still faces hurdles, including winning approval of its arrangement from the Indonesian supreme court and Bre-X shareholders. "I would not say that this is the final hurdle," Barrick spokesman Darcy Pinston said. "But it certainly is a very important one that has been overcome." The mining ministry's approval came with conditions, including that Bre-X form a joint venture with Barrick, rather than just giving Barrick an operating stake. The conditions also said that Bre-X would have to pay Barrick US$20 million for every Busang gold discovery made so far, and US$10 million for every discovery made in the future up to a total of US$130 million. "The conditions imposed on the approval are very onerous," said Bre-X spokesman John Slater. "It's difficult to see how Bre-X shareholders would accept this." Slater said Bre-X would ask the mining ministry to clarify the conditions. Bre-X, which discovered Busang, said it would ask the Indonesian Mines Department to delay setting a deadline for the companies to formalise their arrangement until the mining ministry's conditions are clarified. The deadline for the companies to formalise their arrangement is Dec. 31. Without a formal arrangement, Barrick's operating stake in Busang would be capped at 45 percent, Bre-X said. "We're not going to speculate on what will happen," Pinston said. "But we're working very hard to clarify the situation with the mining ministry and the Mines Department." The Mines Department, which regulates mining operations, has not set a deadline for the companies to formalise their arrangement, a spokesman said. But he said the deadline in the mining ministry's letter was "not a request but a requirement." The uncertainty surrounding the situation sent Barrick's shares down C$1.25 to C$33.75 in heavy trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange. Bre-X's shares fell C$1.10 to C$21.80 in heavy trading on the Vancouver Stock Exchange. Investors were worried that the conditions imposed by the Indonesian mining ministry might not stand up, analysts said. "It's a very precarious situation," said gold analyst Mark Cruise of Research Capital Corp in Montreal. "The Indonesian government has made a lot of demands on Bre-X that Bre-X has not been able to meet. So the question is, will these demands be met or will they be changed?" The Indonesian government took control of Busang last month, saying Barrick and Bre-X had not made sufficient progress towards operating the discovery. The two companies had been locked in a dispute over ownership of Busang, which some experts say contains up to 50 million ounces of gold. Barrick says it has a 35 percent stake in the discovery, while Bre-X says the Canadian company has a maximum of 40 percent. The companies have been trying to work out a deal to let Barrick operate the find and pay Bre-X to reduce its obligation to fund development. But Bre-X shareholders and the Indonesian supreme court must approve any arrangement. In a letter to Barrick on Tuesday, the Indonesian mining ministry said its earlier actions allowing Barrick to operate Busang and approving the companies' arrangement were "annulled." But the ministry then reversed itself and said its earlier actions were "upheld and confirmed." The mining ministry's letter was faxed to Barrick and obtained by Reuters. An official at the Indonesian mines department said the earlier actions against Barrick were annulled and the company must start over. "Barrick has to go through the whole process again," he said. response: The glory of controlling Busang, one of the world's richest gold deposits, has thrown together an unlikely duo. Toronto-based Bre-X Minerals Ltd. and Calgary-based Barrick Gold Corp. have forged a deal that will give Barrick 40 percent of Busang in return for managing and funding development of the deposit. "This is a win-win situation for both companies," Barrick chairman Peter Munk said in an interview Friday. "Bre-X has found a rich ore body. But they need help to develop it." Bre-X, which discovered Busang in Indonesia in 1995, has so far defined the deposit as having 39 million ounces of gold, worth about US$12 billion at current prices. But many experts believe the discovery has a long way to go before its resources are fully defined. "The definition of Busang is just beginning," Bre-X president John Solidonas said in an interview. "We're very pleased to have Barrick come in as a partner." To make the deal work, Bre-X will have to reduce its share of the eventual development and production costs at Busang. Under the arrangement, Bre-X will keep 60 percent and operate the mine. Barrick has an option to increase its stake to 50 percent by spending US$250 million on the property and writing off US$50 million of its investment. To get to a 49 percent ownership, Barrick would have to spend an additional US$200 million on the property and write off another US$50 million. To get to a 40 percent cap, Barrick would have to spend an additional US$1 billion on the property and write off an additional US$150 million. "This is a very aggressive arrangement for Barrick," mining analyst Gilles Dessault of National Bank Financial said in an interview. "But it shows how confident they are in the quality of the deposit." The deal came together quickly. Bre-X and Barrick began talking about a possible alliance in late August. By Friday, they had worked out the details of a deal worth an estimated US$3.8 billion to Bre-X shareholders. The arrangement also calls for Bre-X to give Barrick one out of every four new discovery "bonus" properties in Indonesia. "This is a very good deal for Bre-X shareholders," mining analyst Don McInnes of Research Capital Corp. said in an interview. "But it's a challenge for Bre-X to operate the mine with a 60 percent share." The company has already said that it will find it difficult to attract other investors to buy into Busang without a controlling stake. "I think this deal makes it more difficult for Bre-X to bring in a third party," Dessault said. "But Bre-X has said that they have no plans to bring in a third party." The company has said it wants to develop Busang itself and then move on to its other Indonesian gold discoveries. "This deal does not change our plans for our other properties," Solidonas said. But analysts said it will be difficult for Bre-X to ignore the US$2.5 billion in funding that Barrick will bring to the table. "I think Bre-X will have to rethink its plans for its other properties," McInnes said. The deal also gives Barrick an option to get into any new discoveries Bre-X makes on its existing properties. To keep Barrick happy, Bre-X will have to keep the mining giant informed about its exploration plans. "This is a very good deal for Bre-X," Munk said. "But it's a challenge for them to keep Barrick happy." To do that, Bre-X will have to make some discoveries that Barrick can get into, analysts said. "I think this deal is a good start for Bre-X and Barrick," mining analyst Paul Sinclair of BMO Nesbitt Burns Inc. said. "But both companies will have to make some good discoveries to keep this partnership working." ---- REUTERS Toronto Bureau 416 941-8100 ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- To reach the Toronto bureau, call 416 941-8100. "There is a possibility that (Barrick's) interest in the Torquemada property could offset their interest in Busang," he said. "There's no interest in China right now," a Hong Kong trader said. "It's too high." A Western trader in Singapore said Chinese state stockpiling authorities had not made any inquiries about recent shipments of 20,000 to 30,000 tonnes, and had not asked for any in recent days. "They've been completely out of the picture," he said. "They've been on the sidelines, watching and waiting." China's state stockpiling programme was a major buyer of soymeal in 1995, taking in more than 800,000 tonnes on three separate occasions, before disappearing from the market in late 1996. Prices have risen sharply in recent weeks on the back of a tightening global supply situation and on fund-driven buying of Chicago Board of Trade soybeans and meal futures. A Western trader in Shanghai said China's state stockpiling authorities had been talking to him in recent weeks about the possibility of taking some 200,000 tonnes of soymeal in January. "They asked if we could hold it for them, but we said we couldn't," he said. "We've got nothing booked, and we're not going to," he said. "We're just waiting for the market to come back to us." The lack of interest from China's state stockpiling programme comes at a time when other importers are booking cargoes on the rally. A trader in the Philippines said he was in the process of booking a cargo of 20,000 tonnes of soymeal on prices in the US$310s a tonne C&F. "We've been in talks for a week now," he said. However, the sources said China's steel market was weak and beset by a lack of cash for buyers -- and a rising incidence of contract washouts.
